title: HAMMR-L: Noise Reduction in Quantum Outcomes Using a Richardson-Lucy Deconvolution Algorithm for Quantum State Graphs
summary: Current quantum computers present significant noise, especially as circuit depth and qubit count increase. Prior work has demonstrated that erroneous outcomes exhibit some behavior in Hamming space, enabling improvements in the output distributions of NISQ-era computers. We present HAMMR-L: a principled post-processing technique for improving the fidelity of output distributions by applying Richardson-Lucy image deconvolution on a state graph of measurement results connected by Hamming distance. We show that this preliminary implementation of HAMMR-L outperforms existing cutting-edge Hamming-based post-processors such as QBEEP while being circuit and hardware agnostic, which QBEEP is not. HAMMR-L also demonstrates clear potential for future improvements and we discuss how such improvements might be realized while highlighting the strengths, limitations, and generality of the underlying concept.

AI.tldr: HAMMR-L is a post-processing technique using Richardson-Lucy deconvolution on Hamming-space state graphs to improve quantum computation fidelity, outperforming existing methods like QBEEP while being circuit/hardware agnostic.
AI.motivation: Current quantum computers suffer from significant noise that worsens with circuit depth and qubit count. While prior work shows erroneous outcomes exhibit patterns in Hamming space that can improve output distributions, existing methods have limitations in terms of circuit/hardware specificity.
AI.method: HAMMR-L applies Richardson-Lucy image deconvolution on a state graph where measurement results are connected by Hamming distance. This principled post-processing technique operates in Hamming space to correct erroneous outcomes in quantum computation results.
AI.result: The preliminary implementation of HAMMR-L outperforms existing cutting-edge Hamming-based post-processors like QBEEP. It demonstrates circuit and hardware agnosticism (unlike QBEEP) and shows clear potential for future improvements.
AI.conclusion: HAMMR-L represents an effective post-processing approach for improving quantum computation fidelity by leveraging Hamming-space error patterns. The method's generality, strengths, and limitations are discussed, along with pathways for future enhancements to address NISQ-era quantum computer noise challenges.

title: Quantum Coherence and Giant Enhancement of Positron Channeling Radiation
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Applies Glauber coherent-state formalism to explain the anomalous peak intensity in SLAC positron channeling experiments (Avakyan et al. 1982); predicts N-to-N^2 intensity scaling as an experimental signature
summary: We present a quantum-mechanical calculation of positron channeling radiation in a planar harmonic potential, explicitly accounting for the interference between transition amplitudes from different transverse energy levels. Because the planar channel potential for positrons in diamond~(110) is well approximated by a parabola, the transverse spectrum is equidistant, $\varepsilon_n = Ω(n+\tfrac{1}{2})$, and all $n \to n{-}j$ transitions radiate at the same Doppler-shifted frequency. The entry of the positron into the crystal under the sudden approximation creates a Glauber coherent state with population amplitudes $c_n$. Phase synchronization between the $c_n$ and the dipole matrix elements ensures that all occupied levels contribute constructively to the radiation amplitude, giving an intensity $I_{\rm coh} \propto |A_j|^2$ that exceeds the incoherent (Zhevago--Kumakhov) result by a factor $\mathcal{G} = 12\text{--}31$ for positron energies of $4\text{--}14$~GeV in diamond~(110). Numerical results agree with the experimental peak positions of Avakyan \emph{et al.}~\cite{Avakyan1982}. The enhancement is unique to positrons because their nearly harmonic channel potential is not replicated for electrons. We propose a decisive experimental test of the coherent model based on the predicted nonlinear angular dependence of the peak intensity. The transition from $N$- to $N^2$-scaling of the radiated intensity, driven by quantum coherence, opens a route toward high-intensity monochromatic gamma-ray sources for nuclear physics and materials science.

AI.tldr: Quantum coherence in positron channeling radiation leads to N²-scaling intensity enhancement, enabling high-intensity monochromatic gamma-ray sources.
AI.motivation: To explain the discrepancy between incoherent (Zhevago-Kumakhov) theory and experimental observations of positron channeling radiation intensity, and to explore quantum coherence effects in channeling radiation.
AI.method: Quantum-mechanical calculation using planar harmonic potential approximation for positrons in diamond (110), treating positron entry as sudden approximation creating Glauber coherent states, and analyzing interference between transition amplitudes from different transverse energy levels.
AI.result: Coherent radiation intensity I_coh ∝ |A_j|² exceeds incoherent result by factor 𝒢 = 12-31 for 4-14 GeV positrons in diamond (110), with numerical results matching experimental peak positions from Avakyan et al. (1982).
AI.conclusion: Quantum coherence in positron channeling radiation enables N²-scaling intensity enhancement (vs N-scaling for incoherent case), providing a route to high-intensity monochromatic gamma-ray sources for nuclear physics and materials science applications.

title: Geometric structure of the relativistic quantum phase space
summary: The relativistic quantum phase space (QPS) formalism extends classical phase space by incorporating both mean values and variance-covariance matrices of quantum states, thereby providing a unified setting where the uncertainty principle and relativistic covariance coexist. In this work we explore the basic geometric structure of the QPS for the signature \((1,4)\). We construct a scalar invariant built from the mean values and the inverse variance-covariance matrix, and prove its invariance under linear canonical transformations. For quantum states that saturate the uncertainty relations, and define the QPS itself, the invariant takes a value that encodes two fundamental length scales: a large scale characterising maximal coordinate uncertainties and a small scale characterising minimal coordinate uncertainties. From this invariance we derive a geometric equation that unifies the mean values and the quantum fluctuations. Analysing two asymptotic regimes reveals two physically significant limits: one leads to a curved spacetime geometry, consistent with current cosmological observations; the other yields a curved momenta space structure. These limits suggest a direct connection between quantum phase space geometry, cosmology, and quantum gravity, offering new perspectives on the origin of the quantum structure of spacetime. The results also resonate with the principle of Born reciprocity, which posits a fundamental duality between coordinates and momenta, and align with recent works on the relation between QPS and neutrino physics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a geometric framework for relativistic quantum phase space, identifying invariant structures that connect quantum uncertainty, spacetime geometry, and momentum space curvature, with implications for quantum gravity and cosmology.
AI.motivation: To establish a unified geometric framework where quantum uncertainty principles and relativistic covariance coexist, and to explore connections between quantum phase space geometry, cosmology, and quantum gravity.
AI.method: Construct scalar invariant from mean values and inverse variance-covariance matrix in (1,4) signature QPS; prove invariance under linear canonical transformations; analyze asymptotic regimes for states saturating uncertainty relations.
AI.result: Derived invariant encodes two fundamental length scales; geometric equation unifies mean values and quantum fluctuations; asymptotic analysis yields curved spacetime geometry consistent with cosmology and curved momentum space structure.
AI.conclusion: The QPS geometry provides new perspectives on spacetime quantum structure, connects to Born reciprocity principle, and aligns with neutrino physics, suggesting fundamental links between quantum phase space, cosmology, and quantum gravity.

title: Securing Elliptic Curve Cryptocurrencies against Quantum Vulnerabilities: Resource Estimates and Mitigations
summary: This whitepaper seeks to elucidate implications that the capabilities of developing quantum architectures have on blockchain vulnerabilities and mitigation strategies. First, we provide new resource estimates for breaking the 256-bit Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem, the core of modern blockchain cryptography. We demonstrate that Shor's algorithm for this problem can execute with either <1200 logical qubits and <90 million Toffoli gates or <1450 logical qubits and <70 million Toffoli gates. In the interest of responsible disclosure, we use a zero-knowledge proof to validate these results without disclosing attack vectors. On superconducting architectures with 1e-3 physical error rates and planar connectivity, those circuits can execute in minutes using fewer than half a million physical qubits. We introduce a critical distinction between fast-clock (such as superconducting and photonic) and slow-clock (such as neutral atom and ion trap) architectures. Our analysis reveals that the first fast-clock CRQCs would enable on-spend attacks on public mempool transactions of some cryptocurrencies. We survey major cryptocurrency vulnerabilities through this lens, identifying systemic risks associated with advanced features in some blockchains such as smart contracts, Proof-of-Stake consensus, and Data Availability Sampling, as well as the enduring concern of abandoned assets. We argue that technical solutions would benefit from accompanying public policy and discuss various frameworks of digital salvage to regulate the recovery or destruction of dormant assets while preventing adversarial seizure. We also discuss implications for other digital assets and tokenization as well as challenges and successful examples of the ongoing transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). Finally, we urge all vulnerable cryptocurrency communities to join the ongoing migration to PQC without delay.

AI.tldr: Quantum computing threatens blockchain security; Shor's algorithm can break 256-bit ECDLP with <1450 logical qubits; fast-clock architectures enable on-spend attacks; urgent migration to post-quantum cryptography needed.
AI.motivation: To analyze quantum computing's threat to blockchain security, provide concrete resource estimates for breaking current cryptographic primitives, and identify vulnerabilities in cryptocurrency systems that could be exploited by quantum attacks.
AI.method: Provides new resource estimates for Shor's algorithm breaking 256-bit ECDLP; uses zero-knowledge proof for responsible disclosure; analyzes architecture differences (fast-clock vs slow-clock); surveys cryptocurrency vulnerabilities through quantum lens; discusses technical and policy solutions.
AI.result: Shor's algorithm can execute with either <1200 logical qubits/<90M Toffoli gates or <1450 logical qubits/<70M Toffoli gates; on superconducting architectures with 1e-3 error rates, circuits execute in minutes with <500K physical qubits; identifies systemic risks in smart contracts, PoS consensus, Data Availability Sampling, and abandoned assets.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing poses imminent threat to blockchain security; fast-clock architectures could enable real-time attacks; technical solutions require accompanying policy frameworks; vulnerable cryptocurrency communities must urgently migrate to post-quantum cryptography.

title: Sampling at intermediate temperatures is optimal for training large language models in protein structure prediction
summary: We investigate the parameter space of transformer models trained on protein sequence data using a statistical mechanics framework, sampling the loss landscape at varying temperatures by Langevin dynamics to characterize the low-loss manifold and understand the mechanisms underlying the superior performance of transformers in protein structure prediction. We find that, at variance with feedforward networks, the lack of a first--order--like transition in the loss of the transformer produces a range of intermediate temperatures with good learning properties. We show that the parameters of most layers are highly conserved at these temperatures if the dimension of the embedding is optimal, and we provide an operative way to find this dimension. Finally, we show that the attention matrix is more predictive of the contact maps of the protein at higher temperatures and for higher dimensions of the embedding than those optimal for learning.

AI.tldr: Statistical mechanics analysis reveals transformer models for protein sequences exhibit superior learning properties due to absence of first-order transitions, optimal embedding dimensions, and attention matrices that predict protein contact maps better at higher temperatures.
AI.motivation: To understand why transformer models outperform feedforward networks in protein structure prediction by analyzing their parameter space and loss landscape using statistical mechanics principles.
AI.method: Used statistical mechanics framework with Langevin dynamics to sample transformer loss landscape at varying temperatures, analyzed parameter conservation across layers, identified optimal embedding dimensions, and examined attention matrix correlation with protein contact maps.
AI.result: Transformers lack first-order transitions in loss unlike feedforward networks, creating intermediate temperature range with good learning; layer parameters highly conserved at optimal embedding dimensions; attention matrices better predict protein contact maps at higher temperatures and embedding dimensions than optimal learning dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Transformer architecture's smooth loss landscape enables superior protein structure prediction, with optimal embedding dimensions maximizing parameter conservation and higher dimensions/temperatures enhancing attention matrix's contact map prediction capability.

title: Color code off-the-hook: avoiding hook errors with a single auxiliary per plaquette
summary: Syndrome extraction in the planar color code is complicated by high weight stabilizers and hook errors that can reduce the circuit-level distance. With a single auxiliary qubit per plaquette, any spatially uniform circuit halves the circuit-level distance. We propose a single-auxiliary syndrome extraction circuit with color-dependent gate schedules that avoids all malign hook errors in the bulk, thereby preserving the full circuit-level distance. The circuit has minimal depth: all stabilizers of the same Pauli type are measured in parallel in six time steps. Furthermore, this schedule can be readily applied to the XYZ color code circuit, yielding an improved temporal distance. We find that at the boundary, no single hook error alone reduces the distance; instead, only certain combinations of hook errors do, which we call fractional hook errors. We demonstrate through Monte Carlo simulations over a range of circuit-level noise models and physical error rates that our circuit outperforms the previous state of the art.

AI.tldr: Proposes a single-auxiliary syndrome extraction circuit for planar color codes with color-dependent gate schedules that avoids malign hook errors, preserves full circuit-level distance, and outperforms previous methods.
AI.motivation: Syndrome extraction in planar color codes is complicated by high weight stabilizers and hook errors that reduce circuit-level distance, with existing single-auxiliary circuits halving the distance.
AI.method: Designs a single-auxiliary syndrome extraction circuit with color-dependent gate schedules that avoids all malign hook errors in bulk, measures all stabilizers of same Pauli type in parallel in six time steps, and can be applied to XYZ color code circuits.
AI.result: Circuit preserves full circuit-level distance, improves temporal distance for XYZ color codes, and Monte Carlo simulations show it outperforms previous state-of-the-art across various circuit-level noise models and physical error rates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed circuit provides an efficient, distance-preserving syndrome extraction method for planar color codes that addresses hook error issues and demonstrates superior performance over existing approaches.

title: The different localisation properties of the eigenmodes of the Laplacian and adjacency matrix of 2D random geometric graphs
summary: We compare the spectrum and the localisation properties of the eigenmodes of the Laplacian and the adjacency matrix of 2D random geometric graphs, using numerical diagonalization of these matrices for different system sizes and connectivities. For sufficiently large ensembles of systems, we evaluate the spectrum, the probability distribution of the participation ratio and the relation between participation ratios and eigenvalues. While all eigenmodes of the adjacency matrix are localised for sufficiently large system sizes, the Laplacian matrix always leads to a small proportion of system-spanning modes due to a conservation law, and therefore to power-law tails in the probability distribution of the participation ratio and its relation to the eigenvalues. By disentangling the effects of finite system size, of mean degree, of component size distribution, and of network motifs, we provide a thorough understanding of the data.

AI.tldr: Comparison of Laplacian vs adjacency matrix eigenmodes in 2D random geometric graphs shows adjacency matrix yields all localized modes, while Laplacian produces some delocalized modes due to conservation law.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectral and localization properties of eigenmodes in 2D random geometric graphs by comparing Laplacian and adjacency matrices, investigating how different matrix representations affect mode localization and spectral characteristics.
AI.method: Numerical diagonalization of Laplacian and adjacency matrices for various system sizes and connectivities; analysis of spectra, participation ratio distributions, and eigenvalue-participation ratio relations using large ensembles; systematic disentanglement of finite-size effects, mean degree, component size distribution, and network motifs.
AI.result: Adjacency matrix eigenmodes become completely localized for sufficiently large systems, while Laplacian matrix always retains a small proportion of system-spanning modes due to a conservation law, leading to power-law tails in participation ratio distributions and eigenvalue relations.
AI.conclusion: The fundamental difference between Laplacian and adjacency matrix representations in random geometric graphs stems from the conservation law inherent to the Laplacian, which prevents complete localization and produces distinct spectral signatures with power-law characteristics.

title: Quantum Suicide in Many-Worlds Implies P=NP
summary: In this paper we propose a totally serious algorithm to solve NP problems in polynomial time provided one is willing to wager the fate of all observers in the universe on the many-world interpretation of quantum theory being correct.

AI.tldr: A satirical algorithm claiming to solve NP problems in polynomial time by betting on the correctness of the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics.
AI.motivation: To humorously explore the theoretical implications of quantum many-worlds interpretation for computational complexity, highlighting the absurdity of certain philosophical assumptions in practical computation.
AI.method: Proposes an algorithm that leverages the many-worlds interpretation of quantum theory, essentially "wagering the fate of all observers in the universe" on its correctness to achieve polynomial-time solutions for NP problems.
AI.result: The paper presents a satirical "solution" that only works if one accepts the many-worlds interpretation as literally true and is willing to risk catastrophic consequences across all possible worlds.
AI.conclusion: This is a humorous thought experiment demonstrating that certain interpretations of quantum mechanics, taken to their logical extremes, could theoretically collapse computational complexity classes, but only at unacceptable philosophical and existential costs.

title: Inverse Design of Strongly Localized Topological $π$ Modes in One-Dimensional Nonperiodic Systems
summary: This study investigates the spatial confinement of topological $π$-modes in one-dimensional chiral-symmetric systems. In conventional periodic and quasiperiodic structures, edge-mode wave functions inevitably penetrate the bulk. To suppress this, inverse design of a potential sequence is performed using a generative model under a global topological constraint. The generated sequence reveals a characteristic structure consisting of a topological boundary layer and a macroscopic S-dense domain, leading to enhanced confinement ($ξ=0.85$) while preserving topology. Based on the physical principle extracted from this result, a minimal heterostructure composed of only two S-blocks is manually constructed, which further reduces the localization length to $ξ=0.75$. These results provide a compact design principle for strongly localized topological states.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an inverse design approach to create strongly confined topological π-modes in 1D chiral-symmetric systems by generating potential sequences with topological boundary layers and S-dense domains, achieving enhanced confinement while preserving topology.
AI.motivation: In conventional periodic and quasiperiodic structures, topological edge-mode wave functions inevitably penetrate into the bulk, limiting their confinement. The study aims to overcome this limitation by designing potential sequences that strongly localize topological states while maintaining their topological properties.
AI.method: The authors use inverse design with a generative model under global topological constraints to create potential sequences. They analyze the resulting structure to identify physical principles, then manually construct a minimal heterostructure composed of only two S-blocks based on these principles.
AI.result: The generated sequence reveals a characteristic structure with a topological boundary layer and macroscopic S-dense domain, achieving enhanced confinement (ξ=0.85) while preserving topology. The manually constructed minimal heterostructure further reduces the localization length to ξ=0.75.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a compact design principle for strongly localized topological states in 1D chiral-symmetric systems, demonstrating that carefully designed potential sequences can achieve superior confinement of topological modes compared to conventional periodic/quasiperiodic structures.

title: Non-stabilizerness and U(1) symmetry in chaotic many-body quantum systems
summary: We present exact, closed-form results for the non-stabilizerness of random pure states subject to a U(1) symmetry constraint. Using stabilizer entropy as our non-stabilizerness monotone, we derive the average and the variance for U(1)-constrained Haar random states. We show that the presence of a conserved charge leads to a substantial suppression of non-stabilizerness (magic) compared to the unconstrained case, and identify a qualitative difference between entanglement and magic response. In the thermodynamic limit, stabilizer entropy exhibits a different leading-order scaling close to a vanishing relative charge density, implying that magic is more robust to charge density fluctuations than entanglement entropy. We test our analytical predictions against midspectrum eigenstates of two chaotic many-body systems with conserved $U(1)$ charge: the complex-fermion Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (cSYK) model and a Heisenberg XXZ chain with next-to-nearest-neighbour couplings and conserved magnetization. We find an excellent agreement for the non-local cSYK model and systematic deviations for the local XXZ chain, highlighting the role of interaction locality.

AI.tldr: Exact closed-form results show U(1) symmetry constraints substantially suppress non-stabilizerness (magic) in random pure states, with magic being more robust to charge density fluctuations than entanglement entropy in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.motivation: To understand how symmetry constraints, specifically U(1) symmetry, affect non-stabilizerness (magic) in quantum systems, and to compare the response of magic versus entanglement to conserved charges.
AI.method: Derived exact closed-form results for stabilizer entropy (non-stabilizerness monotone) of U(1)-constrained Haar random states, calculating average and variance. Tested analytical predictions against midspectrum eigenstates of two chaotic many-body systems: complex-fermion Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (cSYK) model and Heisenberg XXZ chain with next-to-nearest-neighbor couplings and conserved magnetization.
AI.result: U(1) symmetry leads to substantial suppression of non-stabilizerness compared to unconstrained case. In thermodynamic limit, stabilizer entropy shows different leading-order scaling near vanishing relative charge density, indicating magic is more robust to charge density fluctuations than entanglement entropy. Excellent agreement for non-local cSYK model but systematic deviations for local XXZ chain, highlighting role of interaction locality.
AI.conclusion: Conserved charges significantly suppress magic in quantum systems, with magic exhibiting different scaling behavior than entanglement near zero charge density. The locality of interactions plays a crucial role in how well analytical predictions match actual system behavior.

title: Pattern Expansion of Spin Glasses
summary: We introduce a systematic method for expanding general spin-glass Hamiltonians in terms of Mattis interactions, providing a novel perspective for understanding the fundamental differences between short-range Edwards-Anderson (EA) and mean-field Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glasses. By iteratively extracting patterns from the coupling matrix, we expand the original spin-glass system into a Hopfield-like model (a series of Mattis interactions) plus a residual system. Our analysis reveals profound distinctions between EA and SK models: while EA models in two and three dimensions break into isolated subconnected sections after expansion, the SK model exhibits remarkable self-similar behavior, with the residual system preserving the mean-field structure and Gaussian statistics throughout the expansion process. This self-similarity manifests in exponential decay of residual matrix norms and expansion coefficients, reflecting the inherent mean-field nature of the SK model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pattern expansion can identify ultra-low energy excitations in EA models, revealing excitations with energies that decrease rapidly with expansion step. Through connected component analysis, we quantify the size-energy relationship of these independent excitation clusters, opening new avenues for understanding the low-energy landscape of spin glasses and providing insights into the nature of metastable states.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a systematic method to expand spin-glass Hamiltonians using Mattis interactions, revealing fundamental differences between short-range Edwards-Anderson and mean-field Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models through pattern extraction and residual analysis.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic framework for understanding the fundamental differences between short-range Edwards-Anderson (EA) and mean-field Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glasses by expanding their Hamiltonians in terms of Mattis interactions, providing new insights into their structural and statistical properties.
AI.method: A systematic method for expanding general spin-glass Hamiltonians using Mattis interactions through iterative pattern extraction from the coupling matrix. The approach transforms the original system into a Hopfield-like model (series of Mattis interactions) plus a residual system, followed by analysis of residual matrix norms, expansion coefficients, and connected component analysis to study size-energy relationships.
AI.result: EA models in 2D and 3D break into isolated subconnected sections after expansion, while the SK model exhibits self-similar behavior with the residual system preserving mean-field structure and Gaussian statistics. The SK model shows exponential decay of residual matrix norms and expansion coefficients. Pattern expansion identifies ultra-low energy excitations in EA models with rapidly decreasing energies, and connected component analysis reveals size-energy relationships of independent excitation clusters.
AI.conclusion: The Mattis expansion method provides a novel perspective for distinguishing EA and SK spin glasses, revealing SK's inherent mean-field nature through self-similarity and exponential decay patterns. The approach enables identification of ultra-low energy excitations in EA models and offers new avenues for understanding spin-glass low-energy landscapes and metastable states.

title: Effects of measurements on entanglement dynamics for $1+1$D $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge theory
summary: The $1+1$ dimensional $\mathbb Z_2$ gauge theory is the simplest model that allows for quantum simulation to probe the fundamental aspects of a gauge theory coupled with dynamical fermions. To reliably benchmark such a system, it is crucial to understand the non-unitary quantum dynamics arising from the underlying non-Hermitian evolution and to model the effects of quantum measurements. This work focuses on measuring physical observables for a $\mathbb Z_2$ gauge theory. Tensor network calculations are performed to probe the effect of measurement for larger lattice sizes (up to 256-site systems). Using Matrix Product State calculations, the dynamics of entanglement entropy are studied as a function of the measurement rate and the coupling constant. We find that, under both local and non-local measurements, the late-time saturation value of the bipartite entanglement entropy remains independent of system size, indicating the absence of a measurement-induced phase transition in the no-click limit.

AI.tldr: Study of 1+1D Z₂ gauge theory with dynamical fermions using tensor networks to analyze measurement effects on entanglement entropy, finding no measurement-induced phase transition in the no-click limit.
AI.motivation: To benchmark quantum simulation of gauge theories with dynamical fermions by understanding non-unitary quantum dynamics from non-Hermitian evolution and modeling quantum measurement effects in the simplest gauge theory model.
AI.method: Tensor network calculations (Matrix Product States) for larger lattice sizes up to 256 sites, studying entanglement entropy dynamics as function of measurement rate and coupling constant under both local and non-local measurements.
AI.result: Late-time saturation value of bipartite entanglement entropy remains independent of system size under both measurement types, indicating absence of measurement-induced phase transition in the no-click limit.
AI.conclusion: The Z₂ gauge theory coupled to dynamical fermions does not exhibit measurement-induced phase transition in the no-click regime, providing important benchmark for quantum simulation of gauge theories with measurement effects.

title: Quantum Optical Neuron for Image Classification via Multiphoton Interference
summary: The rapid growth of machine learning is increasingly constrained by the energy and bandwidth limits of classical hardware. Optical and quantum technologies offer an alternative route, enabling high-dimensional, parallel information processing directly in the physical layer, particularly suited for imaging tasks. In this context, quantum photonic platforms provide both a natural mechanism for computing inner products and a promising path to energy-efficient inference in photon-limited regimes. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a camera-free quantum-optical images classifier that performs inference directly at the measurement layer using Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference of spatially programmable single photons. Two-photon coincidences directly report the overlap between an input image mode and a learned template, replacing pixel-resolved acquisition with a single global measurement. We realize both a single-perceptron quantum optical neuron and a two-neuron shallow network, achieving high accuracy on benchmark datasets with strong robustness to experimental noise and minimal hardware complexity. With a fixed measurement budget, performance remains insensitive to input resolution, demonstrating intrinsic robustness to the number of pixels, which would be impossible in a classical framework. This approach paves the way toward neuromorphic quantum photonic processors capable of extracting task-relevant information directly from HOM interference, with promising applications in remote object recognition, low-signal sensing, and photon-starved biological microscopy.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of a camera-free quantum optical image classifier using Hong-Ou-Mandel interference of programmable single photons to perform inference directly at the measurement layer, achieving high accuracy with robustness to noise and input resolution.
AI.motivation: Classical hardware faces energy and bandwidth limitations for machine learning, while optical and quantum technologies offer high-dimensional parallel processing. Quantum photonic platforms provide natural mechanisms for computing inner products and energy-efficient inference in photon-limited regimes.
AI.method: Uses Hong-Ou-Mandel interference of spatially programmable single photons to create a camera-free quantum optical image classifier. Two-photon coincidences directly measure overlap between input image mode and learned template, replacing pixel-resolved acquisition with single global measurement. Implements both single-perceptron quantum optical neuron and two-neuron shallow network.
AI.result: Achieves high accuracy on benchmark datasets with strong robustness to experimental noise and minimal hardware complexity. Performance remains insensitive to input resolution with fixed measurement budget, demonstrating intrinsic robustness to number of pixels impossible in classical frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Paves way for neuromorphic quantum photonic processors capable of extracting task-relevant information directly from HOM interference, with applications in remote object recognition, low-signal sensing, and photon-starved biological microscopy.

title: Real Variance-Based Variational Quantum Eigensolver for Non-Hermitian Matrices
summary: Non-Hermitian operators naturally arise in the description of open quantum systems, which exhibit features such as resonances and decay processes, where the associated eigenvalues are complex. Standard quantum algorithms, including the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), are designed for Hermitian operators and are ineffective in recovering correct eigenvalues for non-Hermitian matrices. We present a systematic formulation based on a Real Variance-based Variational Quantum Eigensolver (RVVQE) for non-Hermitian operators. A correct cost function that guarantees convergence to the true eigenstates is identified. Our implementation utilizes Hermitian measurements only, rendering the algorithm easily deliverable. The performance and scalability of the proposed algorithm on a hierarchy of dense non-Hermitian matrices of increasing dimension are demonstrated with numerical results and computational metrics.

AI.tldr: RVVQE algorithm for non-Hermitian operators using real variance minimization with Hermitian measurements only.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum algorithms like VQE are designed for Hermitian operators and fail for non-Hermitian matrices, which naturally arise in open quantum systems with complex eigenvalues representing resonances and decay processes.
AI.method: Real Variance-based Variational Quantum Eigensolver (RVVQE) with a correct cost function that guarantees convergence to true eigenstates, using only Hermitian measurements for practical implementation.
AI.result: Demonstrated performance and scalability on dense non-Hermitian matrices of increasing dimensions through numerical results and computational metrics.
AI.conclusion: RVVQE provides a systematic, practical approach for solving non-Hermitian eigenvalue problems on quantum computers using only Hermitian measurements.

title: Process-tensor approach to full counting statistics of charge transport in quantum many-body circuits
summary: We introduce a numerical tensor-network method to compute the statistics of the charge transferred across an interface partitioning an interacting one-dimensional many-body lattice system with $U(1)$ symmetry. Our approach is based on a matrix-product state representation of the process tensor (also known as influence functional or influence matrix) describing the effect of the bulk system on the degrees of freedom at the interface, allowing us to evaluate a multi-time correlation function that yields the moment-generating function of charge transfer. We develop a scheme to truncate non-Markovian correlations which preserves the proper normalization of the process tensor and ensures the correct physical properties of the generating function. We benchmark our approach by simulating magnetization transport within the Heisenberg spin-$1/2$ XXZ brickwork circuit model at infinite temperature. Our results recover the correct transport exponent describing ballistic, superdiffusive, and diffusive transport in different regimes of the model. We also demonstrate anomalous transport encoded by a self-similar scaling form of the moment-generating function outside of the ballistic regime. In particular, we confirm the breakdown of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality in higher-order transport cumulants at the isotropic point. Our work paves the way for process-tensor descriptions of non-Markovian open quantum systems to address current fluctuations in strongly interacting systems far from equilibrium.

AI.tldr: A tensor-network method using process tensor matrix product states to compute charge transfer statistics in 1D interacting lattice systems with U(1) symmetry, benchmarked on Heisenberg XXZ circuits showing various transport regimes.
AI.motivation: To develop a numerical method for computing charge transfer statistics in strongly interacting 1D systems far from equilibrium, addressing current fluctuations that are challenging to study with conventional approaches.
AI.method: Matrix product state representation of the process tensor (influence functional) to evaluate multi-time correlation functions yielding the moment-generating function of charge transfer, with a truncation scheme preserving proper normalization and physical properties.
AI.result: Successfully simulated magnetization transport in Heisenberg spin-1/2 XXZ brickwork circuits at infinite temperature, recovering correct transport exponents (ballistic, superdiffusive, diffusive) and demonstrating anomalous transport with self-similar scaling. Confirmed breakdown of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality in higher-order cumulants at isotropic point.
AI.conclusion: The process-tensor approach enables studying current fluctuations in strongly interacting non-equilibrium systems and paves the way for non-Markovian open quantum system descriptions of transport phenomena.

title: Iterative Optimization with Partial Convergence Guarantees on Neutral Atom Quantum Computers
summary: Neutral atom quantum computers (NAQCs) have emerged as a promising platform for solving the maximum weighted independent set (MWIS) problem. However, analog quantum approaches face two key limitations: constraints of the atomic layout on realizable graph geometries and the absence of performance guarantees. We introduce Lp-Quts, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that integrates an NAQC sampler into a classical cutting-plane algorithm. At each iteration, a relaxed linear program (RLP) bounds the MWIS and induces a reduced graph from which independent sets are sampled using an analog quantum sampler. A novel sample-informed separation problem guides odd-cycle cut selection and accelerates convergence. For t-perfect graphs, Lp-Quts inherits polynomial-time convergence guarantees from the classical theory of cutting planes. We evaluate our approach on instances with up to 300 vertices -- a scale that exceeds the capabilities of current NAQC hardware. In this regime, Lp-Quts reaches solutions within 5--10\% of optimality, outperforming direct analog quantum protocols and greedy baselines under equal sampling budgets. As expected, simulated annealing remains the strongest sample-based solver at this scale. These results demonstrate how quantum samplers can be effectively embedded within classical optimization frameworks to deliver near-optimal solutions with reduced quantum resources while preserving formal guarantees.

AI.tldr: Lp-Quts is a hybrid quantum-classical framework that integrates neutral atom quantum computer samplers into classical cutting-plane algorithms to solve maximum weighted independent set problems with performance guarantees and reduced quantum resources.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of analog quantum approaches for MWIS problems: constraints on realizable graph geometries due to atomic layouts and absence of performance guarantees in pure quantum methods.
AI.method: Hybrid framework integrating NAQC sampler into classical cutting-plane algorithm. At each iteration: solve relaxed linear program to bound MWIS and induce reduced graph, sample independent sets using analog quantum sampler, use novel sample-informed separation problem to guide odd-cycle cut selection for accelerated convergence.
AI.result: For t-perfect graphs, inherits polynomial-time convergence guarantees. Evaluated on instances up to 300 vertices (exceeding current NAQC hardware capabilities), achieves solutions within 5-10% of optimality, outperforming direct analog quantum protocols and greedy baselines under equal sampling budgets. Simulated annealing remains strongest sample-based solver at this scale.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective embedding of quantum samplers within classical optimization frameworks to deliver near-optimal solutions with reduced quantum resources while preserving formal guarantees.

title: Bell's Inequality, Causal Bounds, and Quantum Bayesian Computation: A Unified Framework
summary: Bell inequalities characterize the boundary of the local-realist correlation polytope -- the set of joint probability distributions achievable by classical hidden-variable models. Quantum mechanics exceeds this boundary through non-commutativity, reaching the Tsirelson bound $2\sqrt{2}$ for CHSH. We show that this polytope structure is not specific to quantum foundations: it appears identically in the causal inference literature, where the instrumental inequality, the Balke--Pearl linear programming bounds, and the Tian--Pearl probabilities of causation all arise as facets of the same marginal compatibility polytope. Fine's theorem -- that CHSH inequalities hold if and only if a joint distribution exists -- is precisely the pivot: the instrumental variable model in causal inference is structurally equivalent to the Bell local hidden-variable model, with the instrument playing the role of the measurement setting and the latent confounder playing the role of the hidden variable $λ$. We develop this correspondence in detail, extending it to algorithmic (Kolmogorov complexity) and entropic formulations of Bell inequalities, the NPA semidefinite programming hierarchy, and the MIP$^*$=RE undecidability result. We further show that the Born-rule / Bayes-rule duality underlying quantum Bayesian computation exploits the same non-commutativity that enables Bell violation, providing polynomial speedups for posterior inference. The framework yields a concrete dictionary between quantum information theory, causal econometrics, and Bayesian computation, and suggests new directions including NPA-based quantum causal inference algorithms and quantum architectures for function approximation.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a formal equivalence between Bell inequalities in quantum foundations and marginal compatibility polytopes in causal inference, showing that the instrumental variable model corresponds structurally to Bell's local hidden-variable model.
AI.motivation: To unify seemingly disparate fields by demonstrating that the mathematical structure of Bell inequalities (characterizing local-realist correlations in quantum mechanics) appears identically in causal inference literature, suggesting deeper connections between quantum information theory, causal econometrics, and Bayesian computation.
AI.method: Develops a detailed correspondence between Bell local hidden-variable models and instrumental variable models in causal inference, showing structural equivalence where the instrument corresponds to measurement settings and latent confounders correspond to hidden variables. Extends this correspondence to algorithmic (Kolmogorov complexity) and entropic formulations of Bell inequalities, the NPA semidefinite programming hierarchy, and the MIP*=RE undecidability result.
AI.result: Establishes that Fine's theorem (CHSH inequalities hold iff a joint distribution exists) is precisely the pivot connecting quantum foundations and causal inference. Shows that the Born-rule/Bayes-rule duality in quantum Bayesian computation exploits the same non-commutativity enabling Bell violation, providing polynomial speedups for posterior inference. Creates a concrete dictionary between quantum information theory, causal econometrics, and Bayesian computation.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals fundamental structural equivalence between quantum foundations and causal inference, suggesting new research directions including NPA-based quantum causal inference algorithms and quantum architectures for function approximation. The framework unifies previously separate fields through their shared mathematical structure of marginal compatibility polytopes.

title: Can Quantum Field Theory be Recovered from Time-Symmetric Stochastic Mechanics? Part II: Prospects for a Trajectory Interpretation
summary: In a companion paper we derived a unique time-reversal-invariant stochastic generalization of the Liouville equation and showed that it coincides with the evolution equation for the Husimi $Q$-function in a broad class of bosonic quantum field theories. Here we investigate the prospects for interpreting that evolution equation in terms of underlying stochastic trajectories. Drawing on Drummond's time-symmetric stochastic action formalism, we show that the traceless diffusion Fokker-Planck equation defines a natural measure over stochastic trajectories conditional on mixed-time boundary conditions. However, we identify a significant gap: it has not been established that every $Q$-function can be represented as a weighted average of these conditional probabilities over boundary values. The trajectory interpretation holds for ensembles with fixed boundary conditions but does not straightforwardly extend to arbitrary quantum states. Despite this limitation, we show that Drummond's trajectory dynamics are fundamentally non-Markovian -- a natural consequence of combining stochasticity with time-reversal invariance. This non-Markovianity places the dynamics outside the scope of the ontological models framework and thereby explains why the major no-go theorems for hidden-variable theories do not rule out the approach. These results clarify both the achievements and the remaining challenges in the project of understanding quantum field theory as the statistical mechanics of time-symmetric stochastic processes.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the time-reversal-invariant stochastic generalization of the Liouville equation (which matches the Husimi Q-function evolution) can be interpreted via underlying stochastic trajectories, finding partial success but a key gap in representation.
AI.motivation: To explore whether the previously derived time-reversal-invariant stochastic Liouville equation (equivalent to Husimi Q-function evolution) can be interpreted in terms of underlying stochastic trajectories, connecting quantum field theory to statistical mechanics of time-symmetric stochastic processes.
AI.method: Uses Drummond's time-symmetric stochastic action formalism to show that the traceless diffusion Fokker-Planck equation defines a natural measure over stochastic trajectories conditional on mixed-time boundary conditions, and analyzes the representation of Q-functions as weighted averages of these conditional probabilities.
AI.result: The trajectory interpretation works for ensembles with fixed boundary conditions but cannot be straightforwardly extended to arbitrary quantum states due to an unproven representation gap. Drummond's trajectory dynamics are fundamentally non-Markovian as a consequence of combining stochasticity with time-reversal invariance, placing them outside the scope of ontological models frameworks and explaining why no-go theorems for hidden-variable theories don't apply.
AI.conclusion: The paper clarifies both achievements (partial trajectory interpretation, non-Markovian nature explaining immunity to no-go theorems) and remaining challenges (representation gap for arbitrary quantum states) in understanding quantum field theory as statistical mechanics of time-symmetric stochastic processes.

title: Oxide-nitride heteroepitaxy for low-loss dielectrics in superconducting quantum circuits
summary: Superconducting qubits show great promise for the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computing, but lossy, amorphous dielectrics limit current technology. Identifying highly crystalline and stoichiometric dielectrics with intrinsically low microwave loss is therefore a central materials challenge, yet experimentally validated platforms remain scarce. In this work, we integrate a crystalline dielectric into a heteroepitaxial TiN/$γ$-Al$_2$O$_3$/TiN trilayer grown via pulsed laser deposition. Correlative high-resolution imaging, diffraction, and spectroscopy measurements confirm the single-crystal quality and chemical integrity of all layers, with minimal defects and limited anion interdiffusion across the oxide-nitride interfaces. Using microwave lumped-element resonators with parallel-plate capacitors, we report the first direct measurement of the dielectric loss of epitaxial $γ$-Al$_2$O$_3$, for which we find a low intrinsic two-level system loss, $δ_{\text{TLS}}^0 = (2.8 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-5}$. These results establish heteroepitaxial oxides on transition metal nitrides as an attractive materials platform for superconducting quantum circuits, particularly for integration into compact device architectures such as merged-element transmons and microwave kinetic inductance detectors.

AI.tldr: First direct measurement of dielectric loss in epitaxial γ-Al₂O₃ shows low intrinsic two-level system loss, establishing heteroepitaxial oxides on transition metal nitrides as promising platform for superconducting quantum circuits.
AI.motivation: Superconducting qubits are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but current technology is limited by lossy amorphous dielectrics. There's a need for highly crystalline, stoichiometric dielectrics with intrinsically low microwave loss, but experimentally validated platforms remain scarce.
AI.method: Integrated crystalline dielectric into heteroepitaxial TiN/γ-Al₂O₃/TiN trilayer grown via pulsed laser deposition. Used correlative high-resolution imaging, diffraction, and spectroscopy to confirm single-crystal quality and chemical integrity. Measured dielectric loss using microwave lumped-element resonators with parallel-plate capacitors.
AI.result: Confirmed single-crystal quality with minimal defects and limited anion interdiffusion across oxide-nitride interfaces. Measured low intrinsic two-level system loss: δ_TLS⁰ = (2.8 ± 0.1) × 10⁻⁵ for epitaxial γ-Al₂O₃.
AI.conclusion: Heteroepitaxial oxides on transition metal nitrides represent an attractive materials platform for superconducting quantum circuits, particularly suitable for compact device architectures like merged-element transmons and microwave kinetic inductance detectors.

title: Scalable phonon-laser arrays with self-organized synchronization
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures (SM included). We greatly value feedback, as it provides essential guidance for improving and deepening the quality of our work
summary: Quantum mechanical oscillators operating at frequencies up to the GHz regime have been predicted to support phonon lasing -- self-sustained coherent vibrational motion emerging when the effective gain exceeds intrinsic losses. Current phonon-laser proposals face two key limitations, namely: they lack scalability and rely on coupling all oscillators to a common field, which significantly restricts flexibility and prevents selective, on-demand phonon lasing at specific locations. Given that numerous applications and theoretical insights naturally emerge from scalable many-body systems, addressing these limitations is timely. In this Letter, we demonstrate how scalable arrays of individually addressable phonon lasers can be generated through local driving in a quantum many-body Ising-like spin chain. We rigorously establish the resonance conditions under which mechanical oscillators transition from thermal motion to sustained coherent self-oscillation. Unlike previous approaches that rely on a common coupling bus, our proposal employs purely local driving, resulting in an inherently modular and scalable architecture ideally suited for integration into large-scale quantum systems. Additionally, our approach enables on-demand lasing of individual mechanical oscillators at specific sites by simply switching the spin-mechanical coupling interaction on and off, provided specific resonance conditions are satisfied. Notably, our phonon laser array is robust against resonance mismatches and naturally exhibits both pairwise self-organized synchronization and global phase locking near resonance. Finally, we outline an experimental implementation within current experimental capabilities.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of scalable, individually addressable phonon laser arrays using local driving in quantum Ising spin chains, enabling on-demand lasing at specific sites without common coupling buses.
AI.motivation: Current phonon-laser proposals lack scalability and rely on coupling all oscillators to a common field, restricting flexibility and preventing selective, on-demand phonon lasing at specific locations. Scalable many-body systems are needed for numerous applications and theoretical insights.
AI.method: Uses local driving in a quantum many-body Ising-like spin chain to generate scalable arrays of individually addressable phonon lasers. Establishes resonance conditions for mechanical oscillators to transition from thermal motion to sustained coherent self-oscillation. Employs purely local driving instead of common coupling buses, with on-demand lasing enabled by switching spin-mechanical coupling on/off when specific resonance conditions are satisfied.
AI.result: Demonstrates scalable arrays of individually addressable phonon lasers with modular architecture. The system is robust against resonance mismatches and exhibits both pairwise self-organized synchronization and global phase locking near resonance. Enables on-demand lasing of individual mechanical oscillators at specific sites.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach overcomes key limitations of previous phonon-laser proposals by providing scalability, individual addressability, and flexibility through local driving in quantum spin chains. The architecture is modular, scalable, and suitable for integration into large-scale quantum systems, with experimental implementation feasible within current capabilities.

title: High-efficiency and noise-immune quantum battery
summary: Nowadays, quantum batteries (QBs) have been designed to outperform their classical counterparts by leveraging quantum advantages. For instance, the charging power greatly benefits from the entanglement generation of a collective charging scheme (e.g., the Dicke QB), especially in the ultrastrong coupling (USC) regime or even larger. However, apart from the fragility of the QB under intrinsic decoherence effects, another critical drawback emerges inevitably. Specifically, the non-negligible counter-rotating (CR) term in the USC regime would induce coherence in the energy basis of QB, thus remarkably degrading the charging efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we propose a high-efficiency and noise-immune QB boosted by dynamical modulation. It is demonstrated that the time-varying modulation can effectively reduce the CR coupling, resulting in a notable improvement in charging efficiency. Particularly, for a judicious choice of modulation parameters that entirely eliminate the CR interaction, the Dicke QB can be charged optimally, resembling the behavior of the Tavis-Cummings QB. In the subsequent storage process, beyond the natural robustness to pure dephasing noise, our scenario is also highly resilient to the dissipation noise and thus can achieve perfect energy storage by effective bath engineering. While feasible with current experimental platforms, our proposal offers a solid foundation for the implementation of a powerful QB and may drastically promote the development of energy storage and delivery techniques in the future.

AI.tldr: A quantum battery design using dynamical modulation to suppress counter-rotating terms in ultrastrong coupling regimes, improving charging efficiency and noise immunity.
AI.motivation: Quantum batteries in ultrastrong coupling regimes suffer from reduced charging efficiency due to counter-rotating terms that induce coherence in the energy basis, along with vulnerability to decoherence effects.
AI.method: Proposes a quantum battery boosted by dynamical modulation that reduces counter-rotating coupling, enabling optimal charging similar to Tavis-Cummings models while maintaining robustness to noise through effective bath engineering.
AI.result: Dynamical modulation effectively reduces counter-rotating coupling, improving charging efficiency. With optimal modulation parameters that eliminate counter-rotating interactions, the Dicke QB achieves optimal charging. The design also demonstrates high resilience to both pure dephasing and dissipation noise during storage.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dynamically modulated quantum battery offers improved charging efficiency and noise immunity, providing a foundation for practical quantum energy storage and delivery systems with current experimental platforms.

title: Quantum heat transport in nonequilibrium anisotropic Dicke model
summary: Nonequilibrium heat transport and quantum thermodynamics in light-matter interacting systems have received increasing attention. Quantum thermal devices, e.g., heat valve and head diode, have been realized. Recently, it has been discovered that the anisotropic light-matter interactions can greatly modify the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of hybrid quantum systems, leading to nontrivial quantum phase transitions, quantum metrology, and nonclassicality of photons. To explore the influences of anisotropic light-matter interactions on quantum transport, we investigate heat flow in the nonequilibrium anisotropic Dicke model. In this model, an ensemble of qubits collectively interacts with an anisotropic photon field. Each component interacts with bosonic thermal reservoirs. Quantum dressed master equation (DME) is included to properly study dissipative dynamics of the anisotropic Dicke model. Within the eigenbasis of the reduced anisotropic Dicke system, strong qubit-photon couplings can be properly handled. Our results demonstrate that anisotropic qubit-photon interactions are crucial for modulating steady-state heat flow. In particular, it is found that under strong coupling the heat flow is dramatically suppressed by a large anisotropic qubit-photon factor. While under moderate coupling, the anisotropic qubit-photon interactions enhance the heat flow. Moreover, the increase in the number of qubits amplifies the flow characteristics, with the peaks increasing and the valleys decreasing. Besides, we derive two analytical expressions of heat flows in thermodynamic limit approximation with limiting anisotropic factors. These heat currents exhibit the cotunneling heat transport pictures. They also serve as the upper boundaries for the heat flows in the finite-size anisotropic Dicke model. We also analyze the thermal rectification effect in the anisotropic Dicke model.

AI.tldr: Anisotropic light-matter interactions in the Dicke model significantly modulate steady-state heat flow, with strong coupling suppressing heat flow and moderate coupling enhancing it, while increasing qubit count amplifies flow characteristics.
AI.motivation: To explore how anisotropic light-matter interactions influence quantum heat transport, building on recent discoveries that such anisotropy modifies hybrid quantum system properties and enables quantum thermal devices.
AI.method: Investigation of heat flow in nonequilibrium anisotropic Dicke model using quantum dressed master equation (DME) within eigenbasis of reduced anisotropic Dicke system to properly handle strong qubit-photon couplings.
AI.result: Anisotropic interactions crucially modulate steady-state heat flow: strong coupling dramatically suppresses heat flow with large anisotropic factor, while moderate coupling enhances it. Increasing qubit number amplifies flow characteristics (peaks increase, valleys decrease). Analytical expressions derived in thermodynamic limit show cotunneling heat transport and serve as upper boundaries for finite-size systems.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic qubit-photon interactions are essential for controlling quantum heat transport in light-matter systems, with significant implications for designing quantum thermal devices and understanding nonequilibrium thermodynamics in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Calculating the quantum Fisher information via the truncated Wigner method
summary: In this work, we propose new methods of parameter estimation using stochastic sampling quantum phase-space simulations. We show that it is possible to compute the quantum Fisher information (QFI) from semiclassical stochastic samples using the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA). This method extends the class of quantum systems whose fundamental sensitivity limit can be computed efficiently to any system that can be modelled using the TWA, allowing the analysis of more meteorologically useful quantum states. We illustrate this approach with examples, including a system that evolves outside the spin-squeezing regime, where the method of moments fails.

AI.tldr: New method computes quantum Fisher information from semiclassical stochastic samples using Truncated Wigner Approximation, enabling efficient sensitivity limit calculations for systems beyond spin-squeezing regimes.
AI.motivation: Extend the class of quantum systems whose fundamental sensitivity limits can be computed efficiently beyond current limitations, particularly for systems outside spin-squeezing regimes where traditional methods fail.
AI.method: Use stochastic sampling quantum phase-space simulations with Truncated Wigner Approximation to compute quantum Fisher information from semiclassical stochastic samples.
AI.result: Demonstrated that QFI can be computed from TWA samples, enabling analysis of more meteorologically useful quantum states and systems evolving outside spin-squeezing regimes where method of moments fails.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method significantly expands the range of quantum systems whose fundamental sensitivity limits can be efficiently analyzed using semiclassical stochastic simulations.

title: Direct measurement of the energy spectrum of a quantum dot qubit
summary: The mapping between gate voltages applied to a double quantum dot, and the parameters of a Hubbard-like Hamiltonian, is of utmost importance for understanding and operating spin qubits. State-of-the-art techniques for measuring Hamiltonian parameters (e.g., detuning axis pulsed spectroscopy, DAPS) provide details about energy levels; however, tunnel coupling estimates typically reveal only a small portion of the full Hamiltonian. Here, we demonstrate a Hamiltonian-agnostic technique for measuring the double dot energy spectrum over a wide energy range, at every value of the detuning, called delta-axis spectroscopy (DAXS). We apply the DAXS method to obtain the energy spectrum of a Si/SiGe double quantum dot and use this data to extract the diagonal and off-diagonal couplings of a 15-level Hubbard-like Hamiltonian, demonstrating very good agreement with the experimental measurements.

AI.tldr: Delta-axis spectroscopy (DAXS) enables comprehensive measurement of double quantum dot energy spectra to extract full Hubbard-like Hamiltonian parameters, overcoming limitations of existing techniques.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for measuring Hamiltonian parameters in double quantum dots (like DAPS) provide limited information about tunnel couplings and only reveal partial Hamiltonian details, creating a need for more comprehensive characterization techniques.
AI.method: Developed delta-axis spectroscopy (DAXS), a Hamiltonian-agnostic technique that measures the double dot energy spectrum over a wide energy range at every detuning value, then used this data to extract diagonal and off-diagonal couplings of a 15-level Hubbard-like Hamiltonian.
AI.result: Successfully applied DAXS to a Si/SiGe double quantum dot, obtaining comprehensive energy spectra and extracting Hamiltonian parameters that demonstrate very good agreement with experimental measurements.
AI.conclusion: DAXS provides a powerful, comprehensive method for characterizing double quantum dot Hamiltonians, overcoming limitations of existing techniques and enabling more complete understanding of spin qubit systems.

title: From Promises to Totality: A Framework for Ruling Out Quantum Speedups
summary:
We study when partial Boolean functions can (and cannot) exhibit superpolynomial quantum query speedups, and develop a general framework for ruling out such speedups via two complementary lenses: promise-aware complexity measures and function completions.
  First, we introduce promise versions of standard combinatorial measures (including block sensitivity and related variants) and prove that if the relevant promise and completion measures collapse, then deterministic and quantum query complexities are necessarily polynomially related, i.e., $D(f)=poly(Q(f))$. We then analyze structured families of promises, including symmetric partial functions and promises supported on Hamming slices, obtaining sharp (up to polynomial factors) characterizations in terms of a single gap parameter for the symmetric case and refined slice-dependent bounds for $k$-slice domains.
  Next, we formalize completion complexity as the minimum of a measure over total completions of a partial function, and show that completability of a measure captures the possibility of superpolynomial quantum speedups. Finally, we apply this viewpoint to derive broad non-speedup criteria for some classes of functions admitting well-behaved completions, such as functions with low maximum influence on both the standard and $p$-biased hypercubes and functions with efficiently identifiable domains, and then show some hardness results for general completion techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for characterizing when partial Boolean functions can exhibit superpolynomial quantum query speedups, using promise-aware complexity measures and function completions to rule out such speedups.
AI.motivation: To understand when partial Boolean functions can (and cannot) achieve superpolynomial quantum query speedups, addressing a fundamental question in quantum query complexity about the limitations of quantum advantage for partial functions.
AI.method: 1) Introduces promise versions of standard combinatorial measures (block sensitivity and variants); 2) Formalizes completion complexity as minimum measure over total completions; 3) Analyzes structured promise families (symmetric partial functions, Hamming slice promises); 4) Applies framework to derive non-speedup criteria for specific function classes.
AI.result: 1) Proves that if promise and completion measures collapse, then D(f)=poly(Q(f)); 2) Obtains sharp characterizations for symmetric partial functions via single gap parameter; 3) Derives refined slice-dependent bounds for k-slice domains; 4) Shows completability captures possibility of superpolynomial quantum speedups; 5) Provides broad non-speedup criteria for functions with low maximum influence and efficiently identifiable domains.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a comprehensive framework using promise-aware complexity measures and completion techniques to characterize quantum query speedup limitations for partial Boolean functions, providing both general theoretical results and specific applications to structured function classes.

title: Entanglement between an NV Center and Chiral Photons in a Topological SWCNT Plasmonic Microtoroid
summary: We present a theoretical proposal for a hybrid solid-state quantum node based on a single nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center coupled to a topological single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) plasmonic microtoroid. The SWCNT ring supports deeply sub-wavelength whispering-gallery-like plasmonic modes that are naturally described within a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid framework. Owing to the closed-ring topology, the cavity spectrum contains a zero-mode sector that is tunable by an external magnetic flux through an Aharonov-Bohm shift. We show that the strongly confined CNT near field can exhibit chiral spin-momentum locking, enabling the two circularly polarized NV transitions to couple selectively to clockwise and counter-clockwise cavity modes, while the parasitic linearly polarized $π$-transition is strongly suppressed by the pronounced anisotropy of the local Purcell enhancement. Based on a tripod stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP) scheme, the system can in principle map the NV spin onto a spin-photon entangled state in a deterministic manner, which is then emitted into a side-coupled tapered optical fiber as a tunable flying qubit. We derive the cavity spectrum, the chiral selection rules, the effective tripod Hamiltonian, and the open-system master equation. Quantitative estimates indicate that, under cryogenic conditions and in the overcoupled regime, high-fidelity spin-photon entanglement and in situ magnetic tuning of the emitted photon frequency are in principle achievable. We also discuss a realistic fabrication route for the CNT resonator and deterministic positioning strategies for a single NV center in the CNT near field.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum node combining NV center with topological carbon nanotube plasmonic resonator enables chiral spin-photon entanglement and tunable flying qubit generation.
AI.motivation: To create a solid-state quantum node that can deterministically generate spin-photon entanglement with high fidelity and tunable photon frequency, leveraging the unique properties of topological carbon nanotube plasmonics and NV centers.
AI.method: Theoretical proposal using a single NV center coupled to a topological SWCNT plasmonic microtoroid. The system employs Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid framework, Aharonov-Bohm flux tuning, chiral spin-momentum locking, and tripod STIRAP scheme for deterministic entanglement mapping.
AI.result: Derived cavity spectrum, chiral selection rules, effective tripod Hamiltonian, and open-system master equation. Quantitative estimates show potential for high-fidelity spin-photon entanglement and in situ magnetic tuning of emitted photon frequency under cryogenic overcoupled conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid quantum node offers a promising platform for deterministic generation of spin-photon entanglement with tunable properties, supported by realistic fabrication and positioning strategies for experimental implementation.

title: Change in bit-flip times of Kerr parametric oscillators caused by their interactions
summary: We experimentally investigate how interactions between Kerr parametric oscillators (KPOs) degrade their bit-flip times, where a bit flip is defined as a transition between the two degenerate ground states of a KPO. Interactions between KPOs cause quantum states of KPOs to leak outside the computational subspace, leading to bit flips. Bit flips degrade fidelity and pose a significant problem for KPO-based quantum information processing. We performed an experiment in which a weak microwave signal is injected into one KPO to emulate photon injection from another KPO, and find that the bit-flip time decreases by an order of magnitude due to induced excitations, depending on the frequency and power of the injected signal. Methods to mitigate the decrease in bit-flip times caused by interactions between KPOs are discussed, including adjusting the pump frequencies, coherent-state amplitudes, and couplings between KPOs. These findings provide valuable insights for scaling up KPO-based quantum computers.

AI.tldr: Experimental study shows interactions between Kerr parametric oscillators (KPOs) degrade bit-flip times by an order of magnitude due to quantum state leakage, with mitigation strategies proposed for scaling KPO-based quantum computers.
AI.motivation: Interactions between KPOs cause quantum states to leak outside the computational subspace, leading to bit flips that degrade fidelity and pose significant problems for KPO-based quantum information processing.
AI.method: Experimental investigation using weak microwave signal injection into one KPO to emulate photon injection from another KPO, measuring bit-flip time degradation as a function of injected signal frequency and power.
AI.result: Bit-flip time decreases by an order of magnitude due to induced excitations from interactions, with degradation dependent on frequency and power of injected signal.
AI.conclusion: Interactions between KPOs significantly degrade bit-flip times, but mitigation methods including adjusting pump frequencies, coherent-state amplitudes, and couplings can help address this issue for scaling up KPO-based quantum computers.

title: On the Entanglement Entropy Distribution of a Hybrid Quantum Circuit
summary: We investigate the distribution of entanglement entropy in hybrid quantum circuits consisting of random unitary gates and local measurements applied at a finite rate. We demonstrate that higher moments of the entanglement entropy distribution, such as a ratio between the variance and the mean and skewness, capture nontrivial features of the measurement-induced dynamics that are invisible to the mean entropy alone. We demonstrate that these quantities exhibit distinct and robust behaviors across the volume-law and area-law phases, and can serve as effective diagnostics of measurement-induced entanglement transitions. We propose a phenomenological model describing the effect of measurements in the area-law regime, which, when combined with the directed polymer in a random environment description of the volume-law phase, well matches numerical simulations across the entire phase diagram.

AI.tldr: Higher moments of entanglement entropy distribution reveal hidden features of measurement-induced dynamics in hybrid quantum circuits, serving as effective diagnostics for entanglement phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To understand how measurements affect entanglement dynamics in hybrid quantum circuits and develop better diagnostics for measurement-induced entanglement phase transitions beyond just mean entanglement entropy.
AI.method: Analyze higher moments of entanglement entropy distribution (variance/mean ratio, skewness) in hybrid circuits with random unitary gates and local measurements at finite rates, using numerical simulations and phenomenological modeling.
AI.result: Higher moments exhibit distinct, robust behaviors across volume-law and area-law phases, capturing features invisible to mean entropy alone. A phenomenological model combining measurement effects in area-law regime with directed polymer description in volume-law phase matches numerical simulations across entire phase diagram.
AI.conclusion: Higher moments of entanglement entropy distribution provide powerful diagnostics for measurement-induced entanglement transitions, revealing hidden dynamical features and enabling comprehensive modeling of hybrid quantum circuit behavior across different phases.

title: Multipartite controlled-NOT gates using molecules and Rydberg atoms
summary: We propose high-fidelity controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates in a hybrid system of polar molecules and Rydberg atoms based on the unconventional Rydberg pumping mechanism. By combining the rich internal structure of polar molecules with the strong dipole-dipole interactions of Rydberg atoms, we realize both two-to-one and one-to-two gate configurations. Numerical simulations show that the gate performance is robust against spontaneous emission from Rydberg states. The approach naturally extends to larger systems, as demonstrated by four-qubit implementations achieving three-to-one and one-to-three CNOT gates with fidelities exceeding 99\%. These results highlight hybrid molecule-Rydberg atom architectures as a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Hybrid polar molecule-Rydberg atom system enables high-fidelity CNOT gates using unconventional Rydberg pumping, achieving 99%+ fidelity for multi-qubit operations.
AI.motivation: To leverage the complementary advantages of polar molecules (rich internal structure) and Rydberg atoms (strong dipole-dipole interactions) for scalable quantum information processing, overcoming limitations of single-species systems.
AI.method: Unconventional Rydberg pumping mechanism combining polar molecules and Rydberg atoms, enabling both two-to-one and one-to-two CNOT gate configurations. Numerical simulations validate robustness against spontaneous emission from Rydberg states.
AI.result: Achieved high-fidelity CNOT gates with fidelities exceeding 99% for four-qubit implementations, including three-to-one and one-to-three gate configurations. Performance is robust against spontaneous emission.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid molecule-Rydberg atom architectures represent a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, with demonstrated multi-qubit gate capabilities and robustness against decoherence.

title: YZ-plane measurement-based quantum computation: Universality and Parity Architecture implementation
summary: We define the class of register-logic graphs and prove that any uniformly deterministic measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) where the inputs coincide with the outputs must be driven on such graphs by measurements in the $YZ$ plane of the Bloch sphere.
