This observation is revisited in the context that goes beyond uniform determinism, where we present a universal $YZ$-plane-only measurement pattern and establish a connection between $YZ$-plane-only and $XZ$-plane-only patterns. These results conclude the line of research on universal patterns with measurements restricted to one of the principal planes of the Bloch sphere. We further demonstrate, within the framework of the Parity Architecture, that $YZ$-plane patterns with the register-logic graph can be embedded into another graph with purely local interactions, and we extend this case to the scenario of universal quantum computation.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that uniformly deterministic MBQC with input-output coincidence requires YZ-plane measurements on register-logic graphs, presents universal YZ-only patterns, connects YZ and XZ patterns, and demonstrates embedding into local-interaction graphs for universal quantum computation.
AI.motivation: To characterize the structural requirements for measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) with specific measurement restrictions, particularly when inputs coincide with outputs, and to complete the research on universal patterns restricted to principal Bloch sphere planes.
AI.method: Defines register-logic graphs, proves necessity of YZ-plane measurements for uniformly deterministic MBQC with input-output coincidence, presents universal YZ-only measurement patterns, establishes connections between YZ and XZ patterns, and demonstrates embedding into local-interaction graphs within the Parity Architecture framework.
AI.result: Shows that uniformly deterministic MBQC with input-output coincidence must use YZ-plane measurements on register-logic graphs; presents universal YZ-only patterns; establishes connection between YZ and XZ patterns; demonstrates embedding of YZ patterns into local-interaction graphs for universal quantum computation.
AI.conclusion: Completes research on universal MBQC patterns restricted to principal Bloch sphere planes, establishes structural requirements for specific MBQC scenarios, and provides embedding techniques for implementing these patterns with local interactions in the Parity Architecture framework.

title: PAEMS: Precise and Adaptive Error Model for Superconducting Quantum Processors
summary: Superconducting quantum processor units (QPUs) are incapable of producing massive datasets for quantum error correction (QEC) because of hardware limitations. Thus, QEC decoders heavily depend on synthetic data from qubit error models. Classic depolarizing error models with polynomial complexity present limited accuracy. Coherent density matrix methods suffer from exponential complexity $\propto O(4^n)$ where $n$ represents the number of qubits. This paper introduces PAEMS: a precise and adaptive qubit error model. Its qubit-wise separation framework, incorporating leakage propagation, captures error evolvements crossing spatial and temporal domains. Utilizing repetition-code experiment datasets, PAEMS effectively identifies the intrinsic qubit errors through an end-to-end optimization pipeline. Experiments on IBM's QPUs have demonstrated a 19.5$\times$, 9.3$\times$, and 5.2$\times$ reduction in timelike, spacelike, and spacetime error correlation, respectively, surpassing all of the previous works. It also outperforms the accuracy of Google's SI1000 error model by 58$\sim$73\% on multiple quantum platforms, including IBM's Brisbane, Sherbrooke, and Torino, as well as China Mobile's Wuyue and QuantumCTek's Tianyan.

AI.tldr: PAEMS introduces a precise and adaptive qubit error model that outperforms existing methods by significantly reducing error correlations and improving accuracy across multiple quantum platforms.
AI.motivation: Superconducting quantum processors cannot generate sufficient real-world data for quantum error correction due to hardware limitations, forcing reliance on synthetic data from error models. Existing models either lack accuracy (classic depolarizing models) or suffer from exponential complexity (coherent density matrix methods), creating a need for a more accurate and scalable error modeling approach.
AI.method: PAEMS uses a qubit-wise separation framework with leakage propagation to capture error evolution across spatial and temporal domains. It employs an end-to-end optimization pipeline that identifies intrinsic qubit errors using repetition-code experiment datasets, enabling precise modeling of error correlations.
AI.result: PAEMS achieves 19.5× reduction in timelike error correlation, 9.3× reduction in spacelike error correlation, and 5.2× reduction in spacetime error correlation on IBM's QPUs. It outperforms Google's SI1000 error model by 58-73% in accuracy across multiple platforms including IBM's Brisbane, Sherbrooke, Torino, China Mobile's Wuyue, and QuantumCTek's Tianyan.
AI.conclusion: PAEMS provides a superior alternative to existing qubit error models by offering both high accuracy and practical computational efficiency, addressing critical limitations in quantum error correction data generation and enabling more reliable quantum computing applications.

title: Open Quantum Systems from Dynamical Constraints
summary: Open quantum systems are traditionally described by decomposing the total Hilbert space into a system and an external environment, linked by an explicit interaction Hamiltonian. We propose an alternative framework in which the environment is not introduced as an independent sector a priori, but instead emerges from the dynamical activation of constraints in an initially constrained quantum system. Within Dirac quantization, the physical degrees of freedom define the system, whereas the constraint sector, once promoted to carry its own dynamics, functions as an environment. In this picture, the system-environment coupling is not added through a separate interaction term, but is encoded directly in the constraint structure. As an example, we study a quantum particle coupled to a Brownian-oscillator environment and show how the resulting environmental influence can be formulated in this constraint-based setting. Our results provide a new perspective on the origin of quantum environments and point toward a general framework for open quantum systems rooted in constrained quantization.

AI.tldr: A framework where quantum environments emerge from dynamical activation of constraints in initially constrained systems, rather than being introduced as independent sectors.
AI.motivation: Traditional open quantum system approaches require explicit decomposition into system and environment with interaction Hamiltonians. This paper aims to provide an alternative where environments emerge naturally from constraint structures.
AI.method: Using Dirac quantization, physical degrees of freedom define the system while constraint sector, when promoted to carry dynamics, functions as environment. System-environment coupling is encoded directly in constraint structure rather than added as separate interaction term.
AI.result: Demonstrated with quantum particle coupled to Brownian-oscillator environment, showing environmental influence can be formulated in constraint-based setting.
AI.conclusion: Provides new perspective on origin of quantum environments and points toward general framework for open quantum systems rooted in constrained quantization.

title: Junction-Intrinsic Dissipation in Hybrid Superconductor-Semiconductor Gatemon Qubits
summary: Superconducting transmon qubits based on hybrid superconductor-semiconductor Josephson junctions (gatemons) offer gate tunability, but their relaxation times remain well below those of state-of-the-art transmons, and the origin of this discrepancy is not fully understood. Here, we co-fabricate gatemons and SIS-junction transmons with nominally identical circuit layouts, gate dielectrics, and control lines, so that the Josephson element is the only intentional distinction. Across multiple chips, transmons in this architecture reach relaxation times in the tens of microseconds, whereas gatemons saturate in the few-microsecond range. Using the transmons as on-chip references, we construct a loss budget including Purcell decay, spontaneous emission through the control line, and internal dielectric loss, and find that the corresponding T1 limits exceed all measured gatemon values by more than an order of magnitude. Temperature-dependent T1 measurements follow a common quasiparticle-activation model and yield similar superconducting gaps for S-Sm-S and SIS junctions, indicating that the reduced gatemon coherence is dominated by additional temperature-independent, junction-intrinsic dissipation.

AI.tldr: Gatemons (hybrid superconductor-semiconductor transmons) show significantly shorter relaxation times (few μs) compared to conventional SIS-junction transmons (tens of μs) in identical circuit architectures, with the discrepancy attributed to junction-intrinsic dissipation rather than circuit design or thermal factors.
AI.motivation: To understand why superconducting transmon qubits based on hybrid superconductor-semiconductor Josephson junctions (gatemons) have significantly shorter relaxation times than state-of-the-art transmons, despite offering gate tunability advantages.
AI.method: Co-fabricated gatemons and SIS-junction transmons with nominally identical circuit layouts, gate dielectrics, and control lines, making the Josephson element the only intentional difference. Used transmons as on-chip references to construct loss budgets including Purcell decay, spontaneous emission, and internal dielectric loss. Conducted temperature-dependent T1 measurements following quasiparticle-activation models.
AI.result: Transmons reached relaxation times in tens of microseconds while gatemons saturated in few-microsecond range. Loss budget analysis showed corresponding T1 limits exceeded all measured gatemon values by more than an order of magnitude. Temperature-dependent measurements yielded similar superconducting gaps for both junction types, indicating reduced gatemon coherence is dominated by additional temperature-independent, junction-intrinsic dissipation.
AI.conclusion: The coherence limitation in gatemons is not due to circuit design, thermal factors, or superconducting gap differences, but rather stems from intrinsic dissipation mechanisms within the hybrid superconductor-semiconductor junctions themselves, which require further investigation and mitigation for practical quantum computing applications.

title: Non-perturbative CPMG scaling and qutrit-driven breakdown under compiled superconducting-qubit control: a single-qubit study
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, 43 pages SI, comments/suggestions are welcomed
summary: Decoherence in superconducting qubits emerges from the interplay of multilevel dynamics and structured environmental noise, yet perturbative models cannot capture all resulting signatures. Here, EmuPlat couples instruction-set-architecture-level waveform generation to the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) under $1/f$ non-Markovian pure dephasing. In the resulting non-perturbative regime -- where filter-function predictions become quantitatively uninformative -- CPMG scaling of a three-level superconducting transmon yields one calibration result, two physical findings, and one structural null. Y-CPMG exhibits axis-dependent scaling-law breakdown -- non-monotonic decoherence, partial coherence revival, and pronounced X--Y population asymmetry ($0.204$ vs ${<}\,0.01$) -- driven by third-level anharmonicity amplified by bath memory; X-CPMG maintains well-behaved power-law scaling with a finite-$n$ transient excess consistent with non-Markovian bath-memory effects. The structural null is equally informative: waveform-level differences -- Standard versus VPPU realizations -- remain undetectable across all coupling strengths, establishing that rotating-frame pure-dephasing coupling renders control-layer detail invisible to scaling observables. These findings define testable predictions, the most experimentally accessible requiring only qualitative verification.

AI.tldr: Non-perturbative analysis of superconducting transmon decoherence under 1/f noise reveals axis-dependent CPMG scaling breakdown in Y-direction due to third-level anharmonicity amplified by bath memory, while X-direction maintains power-law scaling with non-Markovian transients.
AI.motivation: Perturbative models fail to capture all decoherence signatures in superconducting qubits arising from multilevel dynamics and structured environmental noise, necessitating non-perturbative analysis.
AI.method: EmuPlat couples instruction-set-architecture-level waveform generation to hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) under 1/f non-Markovian pure dephasing, enabling non-perturbative regime analysis beyond filter-function predictions.
AI.result: Y-CPMG shows axis-dependent scaling-law breakdown with non-monotonic decoherence, partial coherence revival, and pronounced X-Y population asymmetry (0.204 vs <0.01) driven by third-level anharmonicity amplified by bath memory. X-CPMG maintains power-law scaling with finite-n transient excess. Waveform-level differences (Standard vs VPPU) remain undetectable across all coupling strengths.
AI.conclusion: Rotating-frame pure-dephasing coupling renders control-layer detail invisible to scaling observables, establishing testable predictions requiring only qualitative experimental verification.

title: Logical-to-Physical Compilation for Reducing Depth in Distributed Quantum Systems
summary: Quantum computing is expected to become a foundational technology for solving problems that exceed the capabilities of classical systems. As quantum algorithms and hardware technologies continue to advance, the need for scalable architectures becomes increasingly clear. Distributed quantum computing offers a promising path forward by interconnecting multiple smaller processors into a larger, more powerful system. However, distributed quantum computing introduces significant circuit depth overhead, as logical operations are typically decomposed into sequential physical procedures that require entanglement generation. These sequential operations limit the reliability of quantum algorithms in the NISQ era due to noise. In this work, we present a compiler that integrates logical-to-physical decomposition with depth-aware rescheduling to reduce the execution cost of distributed quantum circuits. The compiler identifies sequences of logical CNOT gates that share a control or target qubit, reschedules them into parallel instruction groups, and applies decompositions that allow multiple gates to be executed simultaneously using distributed shared entanglement resources. An algorithm is proposed that ensures parallelism is created when possible while keeping logical equivalence and that circuit depth is never increased. Benchmark results demonstrate that the compiler consistently reduces circuit depth for circuits containing inherently sequential CNOT structures, while leaving already-parallel circuits unchanged. These results highlight the value of combining scheduling and hardware-aware decomposition, and establish the compiler as a practical tool for improving the fidelity of distributed quantum computations.

AI.tldr: Compiler integrates logical-to-physical decomposition with depth-aware rescheduling to reduce execution cost of distributed quantum circuits by parallelizing sequential CNOT gates using shared entanglement resources.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computing offers scalability but introduces significant circuit depth overhead due to sequential decomposition of logical operations requiring entanglement generation, limiting reliability in NISQ era due to noise.
AI.method: Compiler identifies sequences of logical CNOT gates sharing control/target qubits, reschedules them into parallel instruction groups, and applies decompositions allowing simultaneous execution using distributed shared entanglement resources while maintaining logical equivalence and never increasing circuit depth.
AI.result: Benchmark results show compiler consistently reduces circuit depth for circuits containing inherently sequential CNOT structures while leaving already-parallel circuits unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Combining scheduling and hardware-aware decomposition is valuable for improving fidelity of distributed quantum computations, establishing the compiler as a practical tool for NISQ-era quantum computing.

title: Reducing Complexity for Quantum Approaches in Train Load Optimization
summary: Efficiently planning container loads onto trains is a computationally challenging combinatorial optimization problem, central to logistics and supply chain management. A primary source of this complexity arises from the need to model and reduce rehandle operations-unproductive crane moves required to access blocked containers. Conventional mathematical formulations address this by introducing explicit binary variables and a web of logical constraints for each potential rehandle, resulting in large-scale models that are difficult to solve. This paper presents a fundamental departure from this paradigm. We introduce an innovative and compact mathematical formulation for the Train Load Optimization (TLO) problem where the rehandle cost is calculated implicitly within the objective function. This novel approach helps prevent the need for dedicated rehandle variables and their associated constraints, leading to a dramatic reduction in model size. We provide a formal comparison against a conventional model to analytically demonstrate the significant reduction in the number of variables and constraints. The efficacy of our compact formulation is assessed through a simulated annealing metaheuristic, which finds high-quality loading plans for various problem instances. The results confirm that our model is not only more parsimonious but also practically effective, offering a scalable and powerful tool for modern rail logistics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a compact mathematical formulation for Train Load Optimization that implicitly calculates rehandle costs, eliminating the need for explicit rehandle variables and constraints, resulting in a significantly smaller model that remains effective.
AI.motivation: Current mathematical formulations for container loading onto trains are computationally challenging due to explicit modeling of rehandle operations (unproductive crane moves), requiring numerous binary variables and logical constraints that create large-scale, difficult-to-solve models.
AI.method: Developed a novel compact mathematical formulation for the Train Load Optimization problem where rehandle cost is calculated implicitly within the objective function, eliminating dedicated rehandle variables and associated constraints. The approach was evaluated using a simulated annealing metaheuristic on various problem instances.
AI.result: The compact formulation dramatically reduces model size compared to conventional approaches, with formal comparison showing significant reduction in variables and constraints. The simulated annealing implementation finds high-quality loading plans, confirming the model's practical effectiveness and scalability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed compact formulation offers a more parsimonious and scalable approach to train load optimization, providing a powerful tool for modern rail logistics by addressing computational complexity through implicit rehandle cost calculation rather than explicit modeling.

title: Adiabatic Ramsey Interferometry for Measuring Weak Nonlinearities with Super-Heisenberg Precision
summary: We propose an adiabatic Ramsey interferometry technique for detecting weak nonlinearities with trapped ions. The method relies on using the quantum Rabi model as a probe, which is sensitive to nonlinear symmetry-breaking perturbations. We show that the couplings which arise either from anharmonic terms of the trapping potential or due to higher order terms in the Coulomb interaction expansion can be efficiently estimated by measuring the spin state probabilities alone. We show that the spin signal is amplified by the mean-phonon excitations, which results in the estimation precision reaching the super-Heisenberg limit. Notably, achieving such high-precision estimation does not require specific entangled state preparation and can be reached even for initial thermal motion state. Furthermore, we show that the super-Heisenberg scaling can be observed even in the presence of weak spin-dephasing.

AI.tldr: Adiabatic Ramsey interferometry using quantum Rabi model detects weak nonlinearities in trapped ions, achieving super-Heisenberg precision without entangled states or specific initial conditions.
AI.motivation: To develop a sensitive method for detecting weak nonlinearities in trapped ion systems, including anharmonic trapping potentials and higher-order Coulomb interactions, without requiring complex state preparation.
AI.method: Uses adiabatic Ramsey interferometry with quantum Rabi model as probe, measuring spin state probabilities to estimate nonlinear couplings. The technique leverages mean-phonon excitations for signal amplification.
AI.result: Achieves super-Heisenberg limit estimation precision without requiring entangled state preparation, works with initial thermal motion states, and maintains super-Heisenberg scaling even with weak spin-dephasing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adiabatic Ramsey interferometry technique provides a robust, high-precision method for detecting weak nonlinearities in trapped ion systems, overcoming limitations of conventional approaches.

title: Quantum connectivity of quantum networks
summary: The practical utility of a quantum network depends on its ability to establish entanglement between arbitrary node pairs with quality sufficient to execute entanglement enabled tasks. This capability can be assessed globally, through aggregate performance over all node pairs, as well as locally, at the level of individual nodes. Since entanglement-based connections form a layer above the underlying physical topology, quantum connectivity is not adequately captured by classical topological connectivity metrics. To enable characterisation of the quantum connectivity at the level of the network (or its subnetworks), we introduce the quantum connectivity measure (QCM), which quantifies the average connection quality between pairs of network nodes. Further, we describe two quantities, the quantum-connected fraction (QCF) and the quantum clustering coefficient (QCC), naturally derived from the QCM, which capture important features of the functional connectivity of the quantum network at the level of the network and an individual node, respectively. These metrics of quantum connectivity depend crucially on the entanglement distribution protocol and the quantum network parameters in addition to its physical topology. We demonstrate the crucial distinction between topological and quantum connectivity, showing that even a fully connected graph can be functionally disconnected for quantum tasks if average network edge-concurrence falls below a critical threshold. These quantum connectivity metrics thus provide important tools for the design, optimization, and benchmarking of future quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum connectivity metrics (QCM, QCF, QCC) to assess entanglement distribution capability in quantum networks, distinguishing them from classical topological connectivity measures.
AI.motivation: Existing classical topological connectivity metrics fail to capture quantum network functionality because entanglement-based connections operate at a layer above physical topology. There's a need for metrics that characterize the actual ability to establish entanglement with sufficient quality for quantum tasks.
AI.method: Introduces three quantum connectivity metrics: 1) Quantum Connectivity Measure (QCM) - quantifies average connection quality between node pairs; 2) Quantum-Connected Fraction (QCF) - captures functional connectivity at network level; 3) Quantum Clustering Coefficient (QCC) - characterizes connectivity at individual node level. These metrics incorporate entanglement distribution protocols and quantum network parameters beyond just physical topology.
AI.result: Demonstrates crucial distinction between topological and quantum connectivity, showing that even fully connected graphs can be functionally disconnected for quantum tasks if average network edge-concurrence falls below a critical threshold. The metrics provide tools to assess when quantum networks become functionally disconnected despite topological connectivity.
AI.conclusion: The introduced quantum connectivity metrics (QCM, QCF, QCC) provide essential tools for designing, optimizing, and benchmarking future quantum networks by capturing the actual entanglement distribution capability rather than just physical connectivity.

title: Entanglement in prepare-and-measure scenarios without receiver inputs
summary: The most elementary prepare-and-measure scenarios have no independent measurement inputs. No inputs mean that quantum advantages require two indispensable ingredients: shared entanglement and measurements that can be adapted to the communicated messages. Understanding these scenarios is therefore conceptually natural, but also practically relevant, since they act as testbeds for black-box certification of adaptive one-way LOCC. Here, we study them systematically and reveal several of their basic features. For classical messages, we first identify the minimal scenario with a quantum advantage and show that it is maximised by high-dimensional entanglement. Then, we identify the next-to-minimal scenario, and show that quantum advantages can be propelled by nonlocality of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt type, which makes this an appropriate setting for certification experiments. Proceeding further, we replace classical messages with quantum messages, but require the receiver to read the message before measuring the entangled particle. We show that this leads to amplified quantum advantages, that are made possible only thanks to non-projective message read-out. This in dispensable role of non-projective measurements challenges the common wisdom that they play a secondary role in revealing the power of quantum correlations in black-box experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies prepare-and-measure scenarios without measurement inputs, revealing quantum advantages require shared entanglement and adaptive measurements, with classical messages showing advantages maximized by high-dimensional entanglement and propelled by CHSH-type nonlocality, while quantum messages with non-projective read-out enable amplified advantages.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand prepare-and-measure scenarios without independent measurement inputs, which are conceptually natural for studying quantum advantages and practically relevant as testbeds for black-box certification of adaptive one-way LOCC protocols.
AI.method: Systematic study of prepare-and-measure scenarios with no measurement inputs, analyzing both classical and quantum message scenarios. For classical messages, identifies minimal and next-to-minimal scenarios. For quantum messages, requires receiver to read message before measuring entangled particle, focusing on non-projective message read-out.
AI.result: For classical messages: minimal scenario shows quantum advantage maximized by high-dimensional entanglement; next-to-minimal scenario shows quantum advantages propelled by CHSH-type nonlocality. For quantum messages: amplified quantum advantages enabled by non-projective message read-out, challenging conventional wisdom about secondary role of non-projective measurements in black-box experiments.
AI.conclusion: Prepare-and-measure scenarios without inputs reveal fundamental features of quantum advantages: classical messages require entanglement and adaptive measurements with advantages scaling with dimension and nonlocality, while quantum messages enable amplified advantages through non-projective read-out, establishing non-projective measurements as essential rather than secondary in revealing quantum correlations.

title: Non-Equilibrium Sock Dynamics: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in the Agitated Wash
summary: It is a universal empirical observation that socks become unpaired in the laundry. We propose a quasiparticle theory of sock dynamics in which individual socks are modelled as bosonic excitations of the agitated laundry condensate. The sock dispersion relation is material-dependent: nondispersive materials retain their shape, while dispersive materials give rise to the well-documented phenomenon of sock shrinkage. In the convex regions of the dispersive spectrum, socks undergo Beliaev decay and spontaneously split into two lower-momentum socks, while in the concave regions the dominant process is Landau-Khalatnikov scattering, which degrades socks into lint and loose threads. In addition, the rotating drum creates sock-antisock pairs from the laundry vacuum via the dynamical Casimir effect. The coexistence of these creation and destruction channels gives rise to a fundamental ambiguity: an unpaired sock at the end of a wash cycle is equally consistent with the destruction of its partner or the spontaneous creation of an entirely new sock.

AI.tldr: A humorous theoretical physics framework models sock disappearance in laundry as bosonic quasiparticles undergoing quantum processes like Beliaev decay and dynamical Casimir effect, explaining why socks become unpaired.
AI.motivation: To provide a whimsical yet scientifically rigorous explanation for the universal empirical observation that socks become unpaired during laundry cycles, using concepts from condensed matter physics and quantum field theory.
AI.method: Develops a quasiparticle theory where individual socks are modeled as bosonic excitations of an agitated laundry condensate. The theory incorporates material-dependent dispersion relations, Beliaev decay for convex dispersion regions, Landau-Khalatnikov scattering for concave regions, and sock-antisock pair creation via the dynamical Casimir effect from the rotating drum.
AI.result: The theory explains sock shrinkage as a dispersive material effect, sock splitting via Beliaev decay, degradation into lint via Landau-Khalatnikov scattering, and sock-antisock pair creation from the laundry vacuum. These processes create fundamental ambiguity in determining whether an unpaired sock results from partner destruction or spontaneous creation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quasiparticle theory provides a comprehensive, physics-based explanation for sock disappearance phenomena in laundry, demonstrating how quantum field theory concepts can be humorously applied to everyday observations while maintaining scientific rigor.

title: The Manipulate-and-Observe Attack on Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Quantum key distribution is often regarded as an unconditionally secure method to exchange a secret key by harnessing fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics. Despite the robustness of key exchange, classical post-processing reveals vulnerabilities that an eavesdropper could target. In particular, many reconciliation protocols correct errors by comparing the parities of subsets between both parties. These communications occur over insecure channels, leaking information that an eavesdropper could exploit. Currently there is no holistic threat model that addresses how parity-leakage during reconciliation might be actively manipulated. In this paper we introduce a new form of attack, namely the Manipulate-and-Observe attack in which the adversary (1) partially intercepts a fraction $ρ$ of the qubits during key exchange, injecting the maximally tolerated amount of errors up to the 11 percent error threshold whilst remaining undetected and (2) probes the maximum amount of parity-leakage during reconciliation, and exploits it using a vectorised, parallel brute force filter to shrink the search space from 2n down to as few as a single candidate, for an n-bit reconciled key. We perform simulations of the attack, deploying it on the most widely used protocol, BB84, andthe benchmark reconciliation protocol, Cascade. Our simulation results demonstrate that the attack can significantly reduce the security below the theoretical bound and, in the worst case, fully recover the reconciled key material. The principles of the attack could threaten other parity-based reconciliation schemes, like Low Density Parity Check, which underscores the need for urgent consideration of the combined security of key exchange and post-processing.

AI.tldr: A new quantum key distribution attack called Manipulate-and-Observe combines partial qubit interception during key exchange with exploitation of parity-leakage during reconciliation, potentially reducing security below theoretical bounds and fully recovering keys.
AI.motivation: Quantum key distribution's classical post-processing (reconciliation) reveals vulnerabilities through parity-leakage, but no holistic threat model exists for how this leakage could be actively manipulated by adversaries.
AI.method: The Manipulate-and-Observe attack: (1) partially intercepts fraction ρ of qubits during key exchange, injecting errors up to the 11% threshold while remaining undetected; (2) probes maximum parity-leakage during reconciliation and uses vectorized parallel brute force filtering to shrink search space from 2ⁿ to potentially a single candidate.
AI.result: Simulations on BB84 protocol with Cascade reconciliation show the attack significantly reduces security below theoretical bounds and, in worst cases, fully recovers the reconciled key material.
AI.conclusion: The attack principles threaten other parity-based reconciliation schemes like LDPC, highlighting the urgent need to consider combined security of key exchange and post-processing rather than treating them separately.

title: Probes of chaos over the Clifford group and approach to Haar values
summary: Chaotic behavior of quantum systems can be characterized by the adherence of the expectation values of given probes to moments of the Haar distribution. In this work, we analyze the behavior of several probes of chaos using a technique known as Isospectral Twirling [1]. This consists in fixing the spectrum of the Hamiltonian and picking its eigenvectors at random. Here, we study the transition from stabilizer bases to random bases according to the Haar measure by T-doped random quantum circuits. We then compute the average value of the probes over ensembles of random spectra from Random Matrix Theory, the Gaussian Diagonal Ensemble and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, associated with non-chaotic and chaotic behavior respectively. We also study the behavior of such probes over the Toric Code Hamiltonian.

AI.tldr: Analysis of quantum chaos probes using Isospectral Twirling technique, studying transitions from stabilizer to random bases via T-doped circuits, and averaging over random matrix ensembles and Toric Code Hamiltonian.
AI.motivation: To characterize chaotic behavior in quantum systems by analyzing how expectation values of probes adhere to moments of the Haar distribution, using Isospectral Twirling to study transitions between different basis types.
AI.method: Uses Isospectral Twirling technique (fixing Hamiltonian spectrum while randomizing eigenvectors), studies transitions from stabilizer bases to random Haar bases via T-doped random quantum circuits, and computes average probe values over ensembles from Random Matrix Theory (Gaussian Diagonal Ensemble for non-chaotic, Gaussian Unitary Ensemble for chaotic behavior), plus analysis on Toric Code Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The paper analyzes behavior of chaos probes across different regimes: from stabilizer bases (non-chaotic) to random Haar bases (chaotic), with systematic study of transitions via T-doped circuits and comparison across different spectral ensembles including the structured Toric Code Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: The Isospectral Twirling technique provides a framework to characterize quantum chaos through probe adherence to Haar moments, with systematic transitions observable via T-doped circuits and distinct behaviors across different spectral ensembles including both random matrix and structured Hamiltonians.

title: Optimal Control of Spin Squeezing in 2D Finite-Range Interacting Systems
summary: Spin squeezing serves as both a fundamental witness of quantum entanglement and a critical resource for quantum-enhanced metrology. While generating substantial spin squeezing in finite-range interacting systems remains challenging, such capability is important for advancing quantum technologies. In this work, we develop an optimal control strategy for achieving enhanced spin squeezing in a two-dimensional XX model with dipolar interactions. Leveraging rotor-spin-wave theory for periodic boundary conditions, we circumvent computational bottlenecks to explore control strategies at unprecedented scales. Remarkably, optimizing a single collective transverse field is sufficient to achieve substantial squeezing enhancement, exceeding the two-axis-twisting benchmark. The optimized control field achieves this breakthrough by dynamically suppressing inter-subspace mixing induced by the finite-range interactions, thereby confining the system evolution predominantly within the maximal spin subspace. We further extend rotor-spin-wave theory to open boundary conditions and incorporate dephasing noise, providing a scalable framework for realistic systems. Under these conditions, the optimized protocol remains effective, highlighting its robustness and suitability for experimental implementation.

AI.tldr: Optimal control strategy achieves enhanced spin squeezing in 2D dipolar XX model by suppressing inter-subspace mixing with optimized transverse field, exceeding two-axis-twisting benchmark and remaining robust under realistic conditions.
AI.motivation: Spin squeezing is crucial for quantum entanglement witnessing and quantum-enhanced metrology, but generating substantial squeezing in finite-range interacting systems remains challenging, limiting advancement of quantum technologies.
AI.method: Develop optimal control strategy using rotor-spin-wave theory for periodic boundary conditions to circumvent computational bottlenecks; optimize single collective transverse field to suppress inter-subspace mixing induced by finite-range interactions; extend theory to open boundary conditions and incorporate dephasing noise.
AI.result: Optimized control field achieves substantial squeezing enhancement exceeding two-axis-twisting benchmark by dynamically suppressing inter-subspace mixing, confining system evolution within maximal spin subspace; protocol remains effective under realistic conditions with open boundaries and dephasing noise.
AI.conclusion: The optimal control strategy provides scalable framework for achieving enhanced spin squeezing in realistic finite-range interacting systems, demonstrating robustness and suitability for experimental implementation in quantum technologies.

title: Nonequilibrium energy transport in driven-dissipative quantum systems
summary: Nonequilibrium energy transport serves as one of fundamental problems in quantum thermodynamics and quantum technologies. Driven quantum master equation in the dressed picture provides an efficient way of investigating nonequilibrium energy flow in general driven-dissipative quantum systems, where the systems are simultaneously driven by the finite thermodynamic bias and coherent driving field. The validity and general applicability of driven quantum master equation is confirmed by comparing with Floquet master equation, by analyzing energy currents in generic spin and boson models. The additional driving phase reserved in system-reservoir interactions, will apparently modify microscopic energy exchange processes. The steady-state energy currents are dramatically enhanced, in particular near the resonant regimes. In contrast, the traditional dressed master equation yields distinct behaviors of the energy currents. We hope that the driven quantum master equation may provide an efficient utility for the control of quantum transport and thermodynamic performances in driven-dissipative nanodevices.

AI.tldr: Driven quantum master equation in dressed picture provides efficient method to study nonequilibrium energy transport in driven-dissipative quantum systems, showing enhanced energy currents near resonance compared to traditional approaches.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient method for investigating nonequilibrium energy transport in quantum systems that are simultaneously driven by thermodynamic bias and coherent fields, which is fundamental for quantum thermodynamics and quantum technologies.
AI.method: Developed a driven quantum master equation in the dressed picture that accounts for both finite thermodynamic bias and coherent driving fields, with validation through comparison with Floquet master equation and analysis of energy currents in generic spin and boson models.
AI.result: The method shows validity and general applicability, with driving phase in system-reservoir interactions modifying microscopic energy exchange processes and dramatically enhancing steady-state energy currents, particularly near resonant regimes, unlike traditional dressed master equations.
AI.conclusion: The driven quantum master equation provides an efficient utility for controlling quantum transport and thermodynamic performances in driven-dissipative nanodevices, offering improved understanding of energy flow in complex quantum systems.

title: Topological sum rule for geometric phases of quantum gates
summary: We establish a topological sum rule, $ν_U = \frac{1}{2π}\sum_nγ_n = 2mν_H$, connecting the geometric phases accumulated by a two-qubit system over a complete basis of initial states to the winding number $ν_H$ classifying its Hamiltonian. Implementations of the same gate from different topological classes must distribute these phases differently, making their distinction measurable through the Wootters concurrence. As a corollary, nontrivial topology is a necessary condition for entanglement: only Hamiltonians with access to $ν_H \neq 0$ can generate it.

AI.tldr: Topological sum rule connects geometric phases of two-qubit systems to Hamiltonian winding number, enabling topological distinction of quantum gates through entanglement measurement.
AI.motivation: To establish a fundamental connection between topological properties of quantum systems and their ability to generate entanglement, providing a measurable way to distinguish topologically different quantum gates.
AI.method: Develop a topological sum rule relating geometric phases accumulated over complete basis of initial states to Hamiltonian winding number, using Wootters concurrence as measurement tool.
AI.result: Established ν_U = (1/2π)∑_nγ_n = 2mν_H, showing that gates from different topological classes distribute geometric phases differently, making them distinguishable via concurrence measurements.
AI.conclusion: Nontrivial topology (ν_H ≠ 0) is necessary for entanglement generation in two-qubit systems, providing fundamental link between topology and quantum information processing capabilities.

title: Certifying and learning local quantum Hamiltonians
comment: 27 pages. This work subsumes prior works (arXiv:2509.10239, arXiv:2512.09778)
summary:
In this work, we study the problems of certifying and learning quantum $k$-local Hamiltonians, for a constant $k$. Our main contributions are as follows:
  - Certification of Hamiltonians. We show that certifying a local Hamiltonian in normalized Frobenius norm via access to its time-evolution operator can be achieved with only $O(1/\varepsilon)$ evolution time. This is optimal, as it matches the Heisenberg-scaling lower bound of $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$. To our knowledge, this is the first optimal algorithm for testing a Hamiltonian property. A key ingredient in our analysis is the Bonami Hypercontractivity Lemma from Fourier analysis.
  - Learning Gibbs states. We design an algorithm for learning Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians in trace norm that is sample-efficient in all relevant parameters. In contrast, previous approaches learned the underlying Hamiltonian (which implies learning the Gibbs state), and thus inevitably suffered from exponential sample complexity scaling in the inverse temperature.
  - Certification of Gibbs states. We give an algorithm for certifying Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians in trace norm that is both sample and time-efficient in all relevant parameters, thereby solving a question posed by Anshu (Harvard Data Science Review, 2022).

AI.tldr: Optimal certification of quantum k-local Hamiltonians with O(1/ε) evolution time, sample-efficient learning of Gibbs states, and efficient certification of Gibbs states.
AI.motivation: Addressing the challenges of certifying and learning quantum k-local Hamiltonians and their associated Gibbs states, with particular focus on achieving optimal scaling in certification and overcoming exponential sample complexity in previous Gibbs state learning approaches.
AI.method: For Hamiltonian certification: uses time-evolution operator access and Bonami Hypercontractivity Lemma from Fourier analysis. For Gibbs state learning: develops algorithm that directly learns the Gibbs state rather than the underlying Hamiltonian. For Gibbs state certification: creates algorithm that is both sample and time-efficient.
AI.result: Achieved optimal O(1/ε) evolution time for Hamiltonian certification (matching Heisenberg lower bound), sample-efficient learning of Gibbs states avoiding exponential scaling in inverse temperature, and efficient certification of Gibbs states solving Anshu's 2022 question.
AI.conclusion: The work provides optimal and efficient algorithms for certifying and learning quantum k-local Hamiltonians and their Gibbs states, representing significant advances in quantum property testing and state learning with practical implications for quantum verification and characterization.

title: Floquet Codes from Derived Semi-Regular Hyperbolic Tessellations on Orientable and Non-Orientable Surfaces
summary: In this paper, we construct several new quantum Floquet codes on compact, orientable, as well as non-orientable surfaces. In order to obtain such codes, we identify these surfaces with hyperbolic polygons and examine hyperbolic semi-regular tessellations on such surfaces. The method of construction presented here generalizes similar constructions concerning hyperbolic Floquet codes on connected and compact surfaces with genus $g \geq 2$. A performance analysis and an investigation of the asymptotic behavior of these codes are also presented.

AI.tldr: Construction of new quantum Floquet codes on orientable and non-orientable surfaces using hyperbolic tessellations, generalizing previous work on high-genus surfaces.
AI.motivation: To extend quantum Floquet code constructions to more general surfaces (both orientable and non-orientable) beyond the previously studied connected compact surfaces with genus g≥2, enabling broader applications in quantum error correction.
AI.method: Identify surfaces with hyperbolic polygons and examine hyperbolic semi-regular tessellations on these surfaces. The construction generalizes previous hyperbolic Floquet code methods to include non-orientable surfaces.
AI.result: Several new quantum Floquet codes constructed on compact orientable and non-orientable surfaces. Performance analysis and investigation of asymptotic behavior of these codes are presented.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully generalizes hyperbolic Floquet code constructions to include both orientable and non-orientable surfaces, providing new quantum error-correcting codes with analyzed performance characteristics.

title: Trotter Scars: Trotter Error Suppression in Quantum Simulation
summary: Recent studies have shown that Trotter errors are highly initial-state dependent and that standard upper bounds often substantially overestimate them. However, the mechanism underlying anomalously small Trotter errors and a systematic route to identifying error-resilient states remain unclear. Using interaction-picture perturbation theory, we derive an analytical expression for the leading-order Trotter error in the eigenbasis of the Hamiltonian. Our analysis shows that initial states supported on spectrally commensurate energy ladders exhibit strongly suppressed error growth together with persistent Loschmidt revivals. We refer to such states as Trotter scars. To identify such states in practice, we further introduce a general variational framework for finding error-minimizing initial states for a given Hamiltonian. Applying this framework to several spin models, we find optimized states whose spectral support and dynamical behavior agree with the perturbative prediction. Our results reveal the spectral origin of Trotter-error resilience and provide a practical strategy for discovering error-resilient states in digital quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: Trotter errors in quantum simulation depend strongly on initial states, with some states showing anomalously small errors. The paper identifies "Trotter scars" - states on spectrally commensurate energy ladders that suppress error growth and maintain Loschmidt revivals, and provides a variational method to find such error-resilient states.
AI.motivation: Standard upper bounds for Trotter errors often overestimate them significantly, and the mechanism behind anomalously small Trotter errors remains unclear. There's a need to systematically identify error-resilient states for more efficient digital quantum simulation.
AI.method: Used interaction-picture perturbation theory to derive analytical expressions for leading-order Trotter error in the Hamiltonian eigenbasis. Introduced a variational framework to find error-minimizing initial states for given Hamiltonians. Applied this framework to several spin models to validate predictions.
AI.result: Identified "Trotter scars" - initial states supported on spectrally commensurate energy ladders that exhibit strongly suppressed error growth and persistent Loschmidt revivals. The variational framework successfully found optimized states whose spectral support and dynamical behavior matched perturbative predictions.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals the spectral origin of Trotter-error resilience and provides a practical strategy for discovering error-resilient states in digital quantum simulation, enabling more efficient quantum algorithms with reduced Trotter errors.

title: Weak-Field Expansion: A Time-Closed Solution of Quantum Three-Wave Mixing
summary: We present a systematic derivation of the Heisenberg evolution of a trilinear bosonic Hamiltonian system in presence of a strong drive beyond the standard approximation of a classical, undepleted driving field. We employ a perturbative expansion of the Hamiltonian propagator in orders of the input field amplitudes, as opposed to the standard Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff (BCH) expansion of the propagator in orders of time. Our method automatically provides time-closed expressions; and converges considerably faster than BCH, especially in the regime of high parametric gain because the small parameter it uses is natural to the problem. We obtain the well-known quantum solution for optical parametric amplification of down-conversion simply as the first order of the expansion, and present the rigorous procedure to derive higher order corrections one by one. To demonstrate the utility of higher corrections, we discuss the 2nd order correction to the pump field as an ideal detector of time-energy entanglement in parametric down-conversion. We also use the 3rd order correction to calculate the limits on the fidelity of quantum state-transfer from one optical mode to another using sum/difference frequency generation, due to the quantum properties of the strong driving field.

AI.tldr: Systematic derivation of Heisenberg evolution for trilinear bosonic Hamiltonians with strong drives beyond classical undepleted pump approximation using perturbative expansion in input field amplitudes instead of time.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of standard approximations in quantum optics, particularly the classical undepleted pump approximation, and provide more accurate quantum evolution for strongly driven nonlinear systems with high parametric gain.
AI.method: Perturbative expansion of Hamiltonian propagator in orders of input field amplitudes (rather than time via BCH expansion), providing time-closed expressions with faster convergence, especially in high-gain regimes.
AI.result: Obtained quantum solution for optical parametric amplification/down-conversion as first order, with systematic procedure for higher-order corrections; demonstrated 2nd order correction detects time-energy entanglement, and 3rd order correction quantifies quantum state-transfer fidelity limits in sum/difference frequency generation.
AI.conclusion: The amplitude-based perturbative expansion provides superior convergence to standard BCH methods, enables systematic derivation of quantum corrections beyond classical pump approximations, and reveals important quantum effects in strongly driven nonlinear optical systems.

title: LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Algebraic T-Count Optimization
summary: Reducing the non-Clifford cost of fault-tolerant quantum circuits is a central challenge in quantum compilation, since T gates are typically far more expensive than Clifford operations in error-corrected architectures. For Clifford+T circuits, minimizing T-count remains a difficult combinatorial problem even for highly structured algebraic optimizers. We introduce VarTODD, a policy-parameterized variant of FastTODD in which the correctness-preserving algebraic transformations are left unchanged while candidate generation, pooling, and action selection are exposed as tunable heuristic components. This separates the quality of the algebraic rewrite system from the quality of the search policy. On standard arithmetic benchmarks, fixed hand-designed VarTODD policies already match or improve strong FastTODD baselines, including reductions from 147 to 139 for GF(2^9) and from 173 to 163 for GF(2^10) in the corresponding benchmark branches. As a proof of principle for automated tuning, we then optimize VarTODD policies with GigaEvo, an LLM-guided evolutionary framework, and obtain additional gains on harder instances, reaching 157 for GF(2^10) and 385 for GF(2^16). These results identify policy optimization as an independent and practical lever for improving algebraic T-count reduction, while LLM-guided evolution provides one viable way to exploit it.

AI.tldr: VarTODD separates algebraic rewrite correctness from search policy heuristics for T-count reduction, with hand-designed policies matching FastTODD baselines and LLM-guided evolutionary optimization achieving further improvements.
AI.motivation: T gates are significantly more expensive than Clifford operations in fault-tolerant quantum computing, making T-count reduction a critical compilation challenge. Current algebraic optimizers for Clifford+T circuits face difficult combinatorial problems even for structured cases.
AI.method: VarTODD is a policy-parameterized variant of FastTODD that maintains correctness-preserving algebraic transformations while exposing candidate generation, pooling, and action selection as tunable heuristic components. This separates algebraic rewrite quality from search policy quality. The approach is evaluated with both hand-designed policies and automated tuning using GigaEvo, an LLM-guided evolutionary framework.
AI.result: Hand-designed VarTODD policies match or improve FastTODD baselines: reducing T-count from 147 to 139 for GF(2^9) and from 173 to 163 for GF(2^10). LLM-guided evolutionary optimization achieves further gains: 157 for GF(2^10) and 385 for GF(2^16) on harder instances.
AI.conclusion: Policy optimization serves as an independent and practical lever for improving algebraic T-count reduction in quantum compilation. LLM-guided evolution provides a viable approach to exploit this separation between algebraic correctness and search heuristics.

title: Dynamics of entanglement entropy for a locally monitored lattice gauge theory
summary: The $1+1$ dimensional $Z_2$ gauge theory is the simplest model that allows for quantum computation or quantum simulation to probe the fundamental aspects of a gauge theory coupled with dynamical fermions. To reliably benchmark such a system, it is crucial to understand the non-unitary quantum dynamics arising from the underlying non-Hermitian evolution and to model the effects of quantum measurements. This work focuses on monitoring ultra-local physical observables for a $\mathbb Z_2$ gauge theory. Tensor network calculations are performed to dynamically probe entanglement entropy at larger lattice sizes. In this work, we report that continuously monitoring local and diagonal observables (electric and mass energy densities) in the computational basis demonstrates the absence of any measurement-induced phase transition, as indicated by the system-size independence of the late-time saturation value of the bipartite entanglement entropy.

AI.tldr: No measurement-induced phase transition found in monitored 1+1D Z₂ gauge theory with fermions, as entanglement entropy saturation shows system-size independence.
AI.motivation: To benchmark quantum computation/simulation of gauge theories with dynamical fermions by understanding non-unitary dynamics from non-Hermitian evolution and quantum measurement effects.
AI.method: Monitor ultra-local physical observables (electric and mass energy densities) in computational basis for Z₂ gauge theory. Use tensor network calculations to dynamically probe entanglement entropy at larger lattice sizes.
AI.result: Continuous monitoring of local diagonal observables shows absence of measurement-induced phase transition, indicated by system-size independence of late-time saturation value of bipartite entanglement entropy.
AI.conclusion: The monitored Z₂ gauge theory with fermions does not exhibit measurement-induced entanglement phase transitions under continuous monitoring of local diagonal observables.

title: Four Generations of Quantum Biomedical Sensors
summary: Quantum sensing technologies offer transformative potential for ultra-sensitive biomedical sensing, yet their clinical translation remains constrained by classical noise limits and a reliance on macroscopic ensembles. We propose a unifying generational framework to organize the evolving landscape of quantum biosensors based on their utilization of quantum resources. First-generation devices utilize discrete energy levels for signal transduction but follow classical scaling laws. Second-generation sensors exploit quantum coherence to reach the standard quantum limit, while third-generation architectures leverage entanglement and spin squeezing to approach Heisenberg-limited precision. We further define an emerging fourth generation characterized by the end-to-end integration of quantum sensing with quantum learning and variational circuits, enabling adaptive inference directly within the quantum domain. By analyzing critical parameters such as bandwidth matching and sensor-tissue proximity, we identify key technological bottlenecks and propose a roadmap for transitioning from measuring physical observables to extracting structured biological information with quantum-enhanced intelligence.

AI.tldr: A generational framework organizes quantum biosensors by quantum resource utilization, from discrete energy levels to entanglement and quantum learning integration, with roadmap for clinical translation.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensing has transformative potential for biomedical applications but faces clinical translation constraints due to classical noise limits and reliance on macroscopic ensembles, necessitating a framework to organize and advance the field.
AI.method: Proposes a four-generation framework categorizing quantum biosensors based on quantum resource utilization: 1st-gen uses discrete energy levels with classical scaling; 2nd-gen exploits quantum coherence for standard quantum limit; 3rd-gen leverages entanglement/spin squeezing for Heisenberg-limited precision; 4th-gen integrates quantum sensing with quantum learning/variational circuits for adaptive inference.
AI.result: The framework organizes the evolving quantum biosensor landscape, identifies critical parameters (bandwidth matching, sensor-tissue proximity), and reveals technological bottlenecks, providing a structured approach to analyze current limitations and future directions.
AI.conclusion: The generational framework enables systematic advancement from measuring physical observables to extracting structured biological information with quantum-enhanced intelligence, proposing a roadmap for clinical translation of quantum biosensing technologies.

title: High-fidelity entangled photon pairs from a quantum-dot-based single-photon source
comment: 17 pages, main text: 7 pages, 5 figures, supplementary information: 10 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
summary: Entangled photon pairs are a ubiquitous resource in quantum technologies, used in quantum key distribution and quantum networking as well as fundamental tests of non-locality. For scalable quantum networks, pairs that are indistinguishable in all unentangled degrees of freedom are essential, as they enable high-fidelity entanglement swapping across network nodes. To date the most-studied sources of "swappable" entangled photon pairs have been based on spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in non-linear crystals. However, the probabilistic nature and unavoidable trade-off between brightness and unwanted multi-photon emission limits their performance in lossy channels. Here, we demonstrate a high-fidelity source of "swappable" entangled photon pairs using a semiconductor quantum dot (QD) coupled to a tunable microcavity. By actively modulating the QD emission between orthogonal polarisation states, delaying one path in a low-loss Herriott cell, and recombining the two on a balanced beam splitter, we generate entangled photon pairs with a fidelity of $96.1\pm0.5$ %. We identify and mitigate fidelity-limiting factors, achieving a maximum fidelity of $98.1\pm0.5$ % through time-resolved post-selection. The scheme suppresses residual multi-photon events concentrated near the excitation pulse and has only a modest impact on the rate. Furthermore, the photons are mutually indistinguishable, enabling efficient entanglement swapping. Our results establish semiconductor QDs as a viable platform for quantum network-compatible swappable entangled photon pair generation, with feasible entanglement generation rates exceeding 0.5 Gpairs/s.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of high-fidelity "swappable" entangled photon pairs using semiconductor quantum dots with tunable microcavity, achieving 96.1% fidelity and 98.1% with post-selection, enabling scalable quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Current entangled photon sources based on SPDC have limitations: probabilistic nature, brightness-multi-photon trade-off, and performance issues in lossy channels. For scalable quantum networks, indistinguishable photon pairs are essential for high-fidelity entanglement swapping across nodes.
AI.method: Uses semiconductor quantum dot coupled to tunable microcavity. Actively modulates QD emission between orthogonal polarization states, delays one path in low-loss Herriott cell, and recombines the two on balanced beam splitter to generate entangled pairs. Time-resolved post-selection used to mitigate fidelity-limiting factors.
AI.result: Achieved entangled photon pairs with 96.1±0.5% fidelity, improved to 98.1±0.5% with time-resolved post-selection. Scheme suppresses residual multi-photon events near excitation pulse with modest impact on rate. Photons are mutually indistinguishable for efficient entanglement swapping. Feasible entanglement generation rates exceed 0.5 Gpairs/s.
AI.conclusion: Semiconductor quantum dots are established as viable platform for quantum network-compatible swappable entangled photon pair generation, overcoming limitations of SPDC sources and enabling scalable quantum networks with high-fidelity entanglement swapping.

title: Strong converse bounds on the classical identification capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
summary: A strong converse bound for the classical identification capacity of a quantum channel is an upper bound on the asymptotic identification rate of classical messages sent through the channel, such that, above this rate, the probability of an identification error necessarily converges to one. Converse bounds for identification are notoriously difficult to obtain for fully quantum channels. The only previously known converse bound, due to Atif, Pradhan and Winter [Int.~J.~Quantum Inf.~22(5):2440013, 2024], has the unsatisfactory feature of remaining strictly positive even for a completely noisy channel, for which identification is clearly impossible. We derive strong (and hence also weak) converse bounds, for the qubit depolarizing channel with noise parameter $p$, that vanish as $p\to 1$, thereby yielding the correct behavior in the completely noisy limit. Moreover, in the setting of simultaneous classical identification under the constraint of complete product measurements, our converse bound matches the corresponding achievability bound, and establishes that in this case the identification capacity equals the classical capacity of the channel.

AI.tldr: Strong converse bounds for classical identification over quantum channels that vanish in the completely noisy limit, matching achievability for qubit depolarizing channels with product measurements.
AI.motivation: Previous converse bounds for quantum channel identification remained positive even for completely noisy channels where identification is impossible, creating an unsatisfactory theoretical gap.
AI.method: Derived strong converse bounds for qubit depolarizing channels with noise parameter p, ensuring bounds vanish as p→1, and analyzed simultaneous classical identification under complete product measurements.
AI.result: Obtained converse bounds that correctly approach zero in the completely noisy limit, and established that identification capacity equals classical capacity for simultaneous identification with product measurements.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first satisfactory converse bounds for quantum channel identification that exhibit correct asymptotic behavior, resolving a key limitation in previous results.

title: Noise Inference by Recycling Test Rounds in Verification Protocols
summary:
Interactive verification protocols for quantum computations allow to build trust between a client and a service provider, ensuring the former that the instructed computation was carried out faithfully. They come in two variants, one without quantum communication that requires large overhead on the server side to coherently implement quantum-resistant cryptographic primitives, and one with quantum communication but with repetition as the only overhead on the service provider's side. Given the limited number of available qubits on current machines, only quantum communication-based protocols have yielded proof of concepts.
  In this work, we show that the repetition overhead of protocols with quantum communication can be further mitigated if one examines the task of operating a quantum machine from the service provider's point of view. Indeed, we show that the test rounds data, whose collection is necessary to provide security, can indeed be recycled to perform continuous monitoring of noise model parameters for the service provider. This exemplifies the versatility of these protocols, whose template can serve multiple purposes and increases the interest in considering their early integration into development roadmaps of quantum machines.

AI.tldr: Quantum verification protocols with quantum communication can recycle test round data for continuous noise monitoring, reducing overhead and increasing utility for service providers.
AI.motivation: Current quantum verification protocols have trade-offs: classical communication requires large server overhead for quantum-resistant cryptography, while quantum communication requires repetition overhead. With limited qubits on current machines, quantum communication protocols are more practical but still have overhead that can be reduced.
AI.method: Examine quantum verification from the service provider's perspective and show that test round data (necessary for security) can be recycled to perform continuous monitoring of noise model parameters.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the repetition overhead of quantum communication-based verification protocols can be mitigated by reusing test data for noise monitoring, providing dual utility from the same data collection.
AI.conclusion: Quantum verification protocols with quantum communication are versatile - their template serves multiple purposes (verification and noise monitoring), increasing their value for early integration into quantum machine development roadmaps.

title: LO-Free Phase and Amplitude Recovery of an RF Signal with a DC-Stark-Enabled Rydberg Receiver
summary: We present a theoretical framework for recovering the amplitude and carrier phase of a single received RF field with a Rydberg-atom receiver, without injecting an RF local oscillator (LO) into the atoms. The key enabling mechanism is a static DC bias applied to the vapor cell: by Stark-mixing a near-degenerate Rydberg pair, the bias activates an otherwise absent upper optical pathway and closes a phase-sensitive loop within a receiver driven only by the standard probe/coupling pair and the received RF field. For a spatially uniform bias, we derive an effective four-level rotating-frame Hamiltonian of Floquet form and show that the periodic steady state obeys an exact harmonic phase law, so that the $n$th probe harmonic carries the factor $e^{inΦ_S}$. This yields direct estimators for the signal phase and amplitude from a demodulated probe harmonic, with amplitude recovery obtained by inverting an injective harmonic response map. In the high-SNR regime, we derive explicit RMSE laws and use them to identify distinct phase-optimal and amplitude-optimal bias-controlled mixing angles, together with a weighted joint-design criterion and a balanced compromise angle that equalizes the fractional phase and amplitude penalties. We then extend the analysis to nonuniform DC bias through quasistatic spatial averaging and show that bias inhomogeneity reduces coherent gain for phase readout while also reshaping the amplitude-response slope. Numerical examples validate the phase law, illustrate response-map inversion and mixing-angle trade-offs, and quantify the penalties induced by bias nonuniformity. The results establish a minimal route to coherent Rydberg reception of a single RF signal without an auxiliary RF LO in the atoms.

AI.tldr: Rydberg-atom receiver framework for coherent RF signal recovery without local oscillator, using DC bias to enable phase-sensitive detection via Stark-mixed Rydberg states.
AI.motivation: To enable coherent reception of RF signals using Rydberg atoms without requiring an auxiliary RF local oscillator, which simplifies receiver design and reduces complexity.
AI.method: Apply static DC bias to vapor cell to Stark-mix near-degenerate Rydberg pair, creating phase-sensitive loop. Derive four-level Floquet Hamiltonian, analyze periodic steady state with harmonic phase law, develop estimators for phase/amplitude from demodulated probe harmonics, and extend to nonuniform bias via quasistatic spatial averaging.
AI.result: Exact harmonic phase law shows nth probe harmonic carries factor e^{inΦ_S}, enabling direct phase/amplitude estimators. Derived RMSE laws identify phase-optimal and amplitude-optimal bias mixing angles, joint-design criterion, and balanced compromise angle. Bias inhomogeneity reduces coherent gain and reshapes amplitude-response slope.
AI.conclusion: Establishes minimal approach for coherent Rydberg reception of single RF signals without auxiliary RF LO, with theoretical framework validated by numerical examples showing phase law, response-map inversion, mixing-angle trade-offs, and bias nonuniformity penalties.
